title: Volkswagen is cooking up a 'spicy' new electric hot hatch
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Nov 17 2026 - 7:01 am PT
Volkswagen
will reveal the new GTI hot hatch on Friday, promising it will be “something really spicy.”
Volkswagen is launching a spicy new EV hot hatch
To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen is “starting a new chapter,” with its first all-electric model to bear the iconic performance badge.
The ID. Polo GTI “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW said after
opening pre-orders
last month.
Volkswagen previewed a mysterious new hot hatch draped under a cloth that appears to be a souped-up version of the ID. Polo GTI. Despite its attempt to “hide” it, you can see the massive rear wing and wide wheel arches under the cloth.
The company promised that “something really spicy” will be served this Friday, November 20, with the tags #Volkswagen, #GTI, and #GTI50.
Although no other details were revealed, the new hot hatch is thought to be the more powerful “Clubsport” variant.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Volkswagen (@volkswagen)
Volkswagen’s head of driving dynamics, Florian Umbach, told
earlier this year that the company is planning to launch the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, a more powerful variant that will deliver close to 300 hp, up from 223 hp in the standard model.
Umbach said that Volkswagen is developing “a similar kind of paddleshift power delivery that the Hyundai N cars have” for the upcoming electric hot hatch.
Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI (Source: Volkswagen)
Hyundai’s performance EVs, the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, feature a simulated gear-shifting system called N e-Shift that uses paddle shifters on the steering wheel to replicate the feel of an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. It works with the N Active Sound+ system to make it feel like you’re in a traditional gas-powered sports car.
It has yet to be confirmed whether the hot hatch debuting on Friday is, in fact, the new ID. Polo Clubsport, but the design clues give us a good idea of what’s coming.
Volkswagen previews new “really spicy” GTI hot hatch (Source: Volkswagen)
Check back on Friday for the full details.
Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000).
Like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the electric ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 223 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.
In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the
ID.3 GTI
, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

title: Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can't charge at home
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Nov 17 2026 - 6:19 am PT
Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.
The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.
A DC-only car
When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.
That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.
The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.
No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.
For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.
But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.
The fine print makes it worse
As we reported last week,
Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement
requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”
It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.
The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.
subscription agreement
carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.
So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.
Tesla has been teasing the fix for years
The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.
Tesla first showed what looked like
a wireless home charging station
during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.
Tesla then
filed patents for the charging pad
and, after the Cybercab unveiling,
released a video of it charging the robotaxi
at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.
And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even
gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck
last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.
With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.
The other options aren’t great
Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.
Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.
The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered
Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module
last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.
Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.
Electrek’s Take
This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.
Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.
That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.
If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.
The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.
Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it launches, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.
If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. content:
Markets & Policy
Winning solar bids ranged from PLN 180 ($49)/MWh to PLN 377.77/MWh, depending on project size.
Emiliano Bellini
17 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Greenvolt Power and its parent, Greenvolt, developed the Oborniki PV plant in Wielkopolska, Poland. It consists of two 8 MW projects.
Poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) has awarded approximately 1.81 GW of solar capacity in
two renewable energy auctions held on Nov. 9 and 10
The regulator said that photovoltaic projects accounted for 65 of the 68 successful bids in the two auctions, which covered solar and onshore wind installations in two capacity categories.
In the auction for solar and wind projects larger than 1 MW, URE selected 50 bids submitted by 22 developers. The successful projects included approximately 1,799 MW of solar capacity and 64 MW of onshore wind.
A total of 33 developers submitted 61 bids, including 58 for photovoltaic projects. Solar prices ranged from PLN 180 ($49)/MWh to PLN 327.77/MWh, compared with a reference price of PLN 389/MWh.
The auction contracted approximately 17.7 TWh of electricity, equivalent to around 33% of the available volume, with a total value exceeding PLN 5.5 billion ($1.5 billion).
In the separate auction for installations with capacities of up to 1 MW, the regulator selected 18 solar bids submitted by 13 developers, representing approximately 15.6 MW of photovoltaic capacity. No wind projects participated in this category.
Winning prices for smaller solar installations ranged from PLN 320/MWh to PLN 377.77/MWh, against a reference price of PLN 414/MWh.
The auction contracted just under 0.15 TWh of electricity, representing only 1.3% of the available volume.
The results underline the continued dominance of solar in Poland’s renewable energy auction system. Auctions for hydropower, agricultural biogas, and installations using biomass or non-agricultural biogas once again failed to produce any successful bids.
2025 auction round
, URE allocated approximately 1.67 GW of solar capacity and 82.7 MW of wind capacity, with PV accounting for 178 of the 181 successful bids. Winning solar prices ranged from PLN 216.90/MWh to PLN 374.77/MWh across the two capacity categories.
, solar projects secured 198 of the 200 winning bids, including approximately 1.48 GW in the category for installations larger than 1 MW. The two successful wind projects represented 90.8 MW of capacity.
Poland’s renewable energy auctions are part of a support framework for the 2022-27 period that originally targeted approximately 9 GW of new solar capacity and 3 GW of onshore wind.
The country installed approximately 3.6 GW of solar capacity in 2025, bringing its cumulative photovoltaic capacity to around 24.8 GW, according to figures compiled by Agencja Rynku Energii (ARE) for Poland’s Ministry of Energy.

title: Italy surpasses 1 million renewable-linked battery storage systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Italy had more than 1 million electrochemical storage systems integrated with renewable energy installations at the end of October, with combined capacity of 12.84 GWh and power output of 6.5 GW, according to grid operator Terna.
Massimiliano Tripodo
17 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Terna’s latest installed-capacity data show that Italy had 1,004,661 electrochemical energy storage systems integrated with renewable energy installations as of Oct. 31, with a combined capacity of 12,843.76 MWh and power output of 6,497.28 MW.
In October, 13,664 new storage systems were installed, increasing the total by 1.38% from the previous month. New installations added 194.79 MWh of storage capacity, up 1.54%, and 109.40 MW of power, up 1.71%.
Compared with October 2025, the number of renewable-linked battery energy storage systems (BESS) increased by 16.14%, or 139,581 units. Their combined energy capacity grew by 2,045.25 MWh, or 18.94%, while power capacity rose by 1,097.22 MW, or 20.32%.
Terna also reported 25,026 new solar installations in October, adding 864.66 MW of photovoltaic capacity.
New solar capacity installed over the 12 months to October totaled 7,322.52 MW, up 17.5%. The increase from January to Oct. 31 was 5,698.87 MW, or 13.1%.
Italy now has 2,255,225 photovoltaic installations across all system sizes, representing 99.4% of renewable energy installations. Solar accounts for 49,211.85 MW, or 54.84%, of the country’s total renewable energy capacity.
For comparison, Terna recorded 40,333 new solar installations in September, adding 656.80 MW. In 2025, Italy installed 213,200 photovoltaic systems with a combined capacity of 6.4 GW.

title: Amazon to invest $7 billion in renewable energy in India by 2030 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Amazon also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined total capacity of 934 MW in India. The projects have been secured through power purchase agreements (PPAs) and are part of Amazon’s existing $4 billion contracted projects in India.
Uma Gupta
17 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Amazon today announced plans to invest $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, significantly expanding its renewable energy portfolio. This is in addition to the $4 billion in renewable energy investments already committed, positioning Amazon among India’s leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free electricity.
Amazon also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined total capacity of 934 MW in India. These include a 234 MW wind farm in Bijapur, Karnataka, to be developed by Sunsure, marking Amazon’s largest wind project contracted in Asia to date; a 200 MW hybrid solar and wind project in Tumkur, Karnataka, also to be developed by Sunsure; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh to be developed by Waaree; and a 200 MW solar project in Dinkar, Rajasthan, to be developed by ReNew.
The projects have been secured through power purchase agreements (PPAs) and are part of Amazon’s existing $4 billion contracted projects in India.
Amazon’s renewable energy investments in India will contribute to its new global target to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65% by 2030.
“We welcome Amazon’s continued investment in renewable energy in India. Such investments play an important role in advancing India’s clean energy ambitions, strengthening energy security and supporting sustainable economic growth. They also demonstrate the growing confidence of global companies in India’s renewable energy sector and its potential to attract long-term investment, create economic opportunities and accelerate the country’s energy transition. We look forward to continued collaboration with industry to advance India’s renewable energy goals,” said Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Pralhad Joshi.
“Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry. This additional investment of $7 billion underlines our long-term commitment, helping bring additional wind and solar capacity online while contributing to India’s energy security and long-term renewable energy ambitions,” said Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer, Amazon. “By expanding access to renewable energy at scale, we aim to help meet India’s growing electricity demand, strengthen the country’s energy security and contribute to its ambitious goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2070.”

title: German companies develop safety concept for inverter-free plug-in battery storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The proposed system combines cell-level power electronics with real-time circuit monitoring to prevent household wiring from overheating. Each module will offer 2 kWh to 5 kWh of storage capacity, with integrated grid protection and emergency power functionality.
Sandra Enkhardt
17 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
Indielux GmbH, a developer of plug-in solar and storage safety technology, and p&e power&energy GmbH, a specialist in battery power electronics, have signed a memorandum of understanding to implement a jointly developed safety concept for modular plug-in battery storage systems.
The concept combines p&e’s multilevel technology, which generates alternating current (AC) directly at the battery cell level without a central inverter, with Indielux’s patented ready2plugin safety technology. The companies say the combination is designed to prevent household electrical wiring from overheating.
According to the companies, this is particularly important for plug-in storage systems installed in living spaces or on balconies, where stringent safety requirements apply. Conventional circuit breakers typically detect current drawn from the grid but do not account for additional power fed into household circuits by storage systems. This can cause wiring to overheat and damage PVC insulation.
“If a storage system continuously feeds an additional 800 W into the circuit, the wiring could reach a critical state in just about six months. At 2,500 W, the wiring becomes so hot that the insulation begins to decompose, posing a fire hazard,” the companies said.
Indielux’s ready2plugin technology monitors electrical circuits in real time and disconnects the power supply before the wiring overheats. According to the company, the maximum amount of electricity that can be fed into a household circuit through a standard socket without additional overload protection is 1,200 kWh per year. With ready2plugin, that figure can increase to as much as 22,800 kWh per year, according to the company.
P&e’s power electronics platform incorporates a dedicated switching stage for each battery cell, allowing the system to switch voltages of just a few volts rather than several hundred volts. The architecture eliminates the need for a central inverter, enables weaker cells to be bypassed and minimizes switching losses. According to p&e, the power electronics achieve efficiency levels exceeding 99%. Under moderate loads, the modules require no cooling fan and can also be installed outdoors, depending on the battery chemistry and enclosure design.
“Plug-in storage systems are becoming increasingly powerful, yet the household electrical wiring remains the same,” said Marcus Vietzke, managing director of Indielux. “That is why circuit protection must be integrated into every module from the very start. The concept is set. Now, we are building the safest and most efficient plug-in storage system.”
The companies plan to begin by testing the integration of ready2plugin technology into p&e’s storage systems. Under the proposed design, each module will function as a standalone storage unit, with a capacity of 2 kWh to 5 kWh, an output of up to 2.3 kW and integrated grid and circuit protection.
Multiple modules will be able to feed up to 2.6 kW into a household circuit through a single socket. In the event of a grid outage, the companies say the integrated emergency power outlets will provide a combined output of up to 4.6 kW.
The jointly developed safety concept includes 24 technical measures aimed at meeting VDE standards for personal safety, electrical wiring protection and grid protection.

title: Sunkean unveils ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-T system at RE+ - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The manufacturer’s trunk system and factory-assembled PV wire harnesses are designed to simplify DC cable routing and reduce field wiring, offering configurable power collection options for different module arrangements and utility-scale solar plant layouts.
Sunkean Cable
17 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Utility-scale
For utility-scale PV projects, the DC collection network influences both construction efficiency and long-term connection reliability. Across large arrays, cable routing and repeated wiring operations require careful coordination. SUNKEAN addresses these challenges through two product groups: factory-assembled trunk systems and PV wire harnesses.
At RE+, SUNKEAN officially launched its ETL-certified 2000 VDC TRUNK-T
system, extending its pre-assembled collection portfolio to higher-voltage applications. Designed for large ground-mounted solar plants, the system integrates trunk cables and branch connections into a single assembly that collects DC power from PV strings and delivers it to a disconnect box.
supports customized configurations to accommodate string positions, equipment locations, and project-specific layouts. Its vertical cable exits facilitate branch cable routing, helping installers follow the planned collection layout. Factory pre-assembly reduces the number of individual connection tasks performed on site, helping standardize connection work across the array.
The system’s current collection architecture addresses a separate concern: localized temperature rise. Where several branch currents converge directly at one point on the trunk conductor, this concentration of current can lead to localized heating. TRUNK-T
instead uses a staged approach, combining incoming branch currents before feeding the combined current into the trunk cable. This design is intended to reduce the risk of excessive localized temperature rise.
SUNKEAN also offers copper-to-aluminum and all-aluminum options, giving customers greater flexibility to select conductors in line with the project’s electrical design and material requirements.
Alongside its trunk system, SUNKEAN offers PV wire harnesses with multiple branch configurations, including S-Y, S-X, and S-T designs, to accommodate different module layouts. Factory assembly helps reduce connection errors and maintain consistent installation quality. Matching the harness configuration to the module layout before construction also helps contractors prepare for installation.
For EPC contractors, the combined portfolio helps plan wiring assemblies around the project layout and better manage on-site workloads. For developers, it offers a way to balance construction costs with the need for reliable DC connections throughout the plant’s operating life.
SUNKEAN’s product innovations reflect its commitment to advancing solar connectivity. By addressing both construction needs and connection performance, the company aims to help customers build more reliable PV systems that support stable, long-term operation and greater sustainability.

pv magazine
reported on Oct. 28
. Chile’s National Electric Coordinator (Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional) has confirmed that it activated disconnection protocols to protect the grid and that an investigation remains ongoing.
On Nov. 11, Chilean lawmaker Cristián Araya Lerdo de Tejada submitted two formal requests for information to the ministries of Public Security and Energy, seeking clarification on the circumstances surrounding the incident and the measures taken in response.
According to the Coordinator’s daily report for Nov. 14, both the solar plant and the BESS had 0% availability and remained listed as forced disconnections. The report cites the same cause recorded on Aug. 27, under forced disconnection request SDCF 2026100475, attributing the outage to a cyberattack targeting the Huatacondo facilities. The BESS is still undergoing commissioning, meaning its unavailability does not constitute an interruption of commercial operations.
In comments reported by Chilean broadcaster T13, Patricio Leyton, cybersecurity director at the National Electric Coordinator, said the organization activated its disconnection protocol to safeguard the electricity system after receiving information from the affected company.
The Coordinator described the incident as exceptional and said it continues to receive updates on the investigation, but declined to provide further details, citing confidentiality. T13 dated the attack to Aug. 26, while the Coordinator’s operational records show that a disconnection request was filed on Aug. 27.
The T13 report also said two other suspected cyberattacks involving facilities in the Coquimbo region had subsequently been ruled out. On Aug. 27, the Coordinator’s records attributed the loss of monitoring and remote-control capabilities at the Olivos and Espinos thermal power plants in Los Vilos to a cyberattack.
This represents a development from the account published by
pv magazine
on Oct. 28, although no independent documentary confirmation of the dismissal of those incidents has been found. On the same day, a forced disconnection was also requested for the 220/23 kV TR1 transformer at the Santa Rita substation, with a cyberattack cited as the cause.
Against this backdrop, Araya submitted two formal requests for information through the Chamber of Deputies, numbered 28298 and 28300.
The first, addressed to the Ministry of Public Security, asks the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) to provide information on the incidents and verify whether the companies operating the affected facilities, as well as the Coordinator, complied with the notification requirements under Chile’s Framework Cybersecurity Law.
The law requires an initial alert within three hours of becoming aware of an incident with a potentially significant impact, an update within 72 hours and a final report within 15 calendar days.
The second request, addressed to the Ministry of Energy, seeks clarification on whether the incidents’ cyber-related origins have been technically confirmed, whether any connection between them has been established and which systems were compromised.
It specifically refers to supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, remote-control equipment, electrical protection systems, inverters and BESS management systems.
The request also seeks information on potential unauthorized remote access, the operational and economic impact of the incident, preventive measures implemented at other renewable energy and storage facilities, and the expected timeline for reconnecting the Huatacondo plant.
Araya also requested an update on the Technical Standard for Cybersecurity and Information Security for the electricity sector, which Chile’s National Energy Commission submitted for public consultation in August.
As of Nov. 16, the Chamber of Deputies had recorded no response to either request. No technical findings have been publicly released regarding the origin of the Huatacondo cyberattack, the specific systems affected or a confirmed date for the resumption of operations at the solar plant and its battery storage system.

title: Dutch researchers develop LEGO-like solar blocks combining luminescent concentrators and perovskite PV cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
The integration of perovskite PV cells will enable the colourful blocks to convert concentrated light into electricity, with expected efficiencies below 10%. Initial applications will target educational kits, with longer-term potential for building-integrated photovoltaics and urban infrastructure.
Emiliano Bellini
17 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Prototype of a LEGO-like luminescent solar concentrator block designed to channel absorbed light toward integrated photovoltaic cells.
Researchers at
Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e)
are developing colourful, LEGO-like building blocks capable of harvesting sunlight and converting it into electricity. The technology uses luminescent solar concentrators (LSCs) combined with photovoltaic cells, potentially opening up new opportunities for solar-powered educational toys, urban infrastructure and building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV).
The blocks are made from transparent polymers containing fluorescent dyes that absorb incoming light and re-emit it at longer wavelengths, according to lead researcher Martijn van Best. “The dyes absorb specific wavelengths of incident light, whether sunlight or interior, artificial lighting, and re-emit this light at a longer wavelength,” he told
pv magazine
. The light is then guided towards the edges of the blocks through total internal reflection, where photovoltaic cells can convert it into electricity.
“At one side of the block, we will attach customized photovoltaic cells, initially perovskite devices, to convert the emission light into electrical current,” Van Best said. He noted that the technology can operate under a range of lighting conditions, including indoors. “A distinct advantage of the luminescent solar concentrators (LSCs) is that they function well in both direct and indirect sunlight.”
Van Best also noted that the colour of the blocks will influence their performance. “They are also tough and colorful, although the color will affect electrical performance: red blocks will be more efficient than blue, for example,” he said.
The researchers expect the devices to achieve electrical conversion efficiencies below 10%, significantly lower than those of conventional crystalline silicon solar cells. Nevertheless, Van Best stressed that efficiency should not be the primary criterion for evaluating the technology, as the blocks are designed to combine electricity generation with other functions.
“Solar cells will always be more efficient than an LSC device, but the LSC has a different purpose, and is not only for generating electricity,” he said.
He pointed to previous applications of LSC technology in solar noise barriers, where sound insulation, appearance and transparency were more important than electricity generation. Similar principles could apply to bus shelters, urban furniture and building materials, allowing otherwise passive structures to generate power.
“So, efficiencies are expected to be modest but enough to power small objects locally such as LEDs or little motors in the case of the toy blocks, a bus shelter message board or advertising sign, without having to hide an unattractive solar panel or fear of it being stolen,” Van Best explained.
The project remains at an early development stage. Initial research conducted by two master’s students has resulted in yellow and red blocks made from polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a transparent silicone polymer. The team has also developed optical simulations to predict their performance.
The researchers are now investigating how stacking multiple blocks affects light transmission and electricity generation. Another challenge involves integrating photovoltaic cells and electrical connections into an interlocking structure without compromising optical performance.
Van Best said Canadian project partner Block&Code has already addressed several electrical interconnection challenges, although further development is required to accommodate solar cells and optimise light guidance. The team must also establish dedicated measurement methods for three-dimensional LSC structures, an area that has received limited previous research attention.
The first practical applications are expected to involve educational products rather than large-scale construction. The researchers aim to incorporate solar-powered blocks into the SparkBlocks range of children’s educational kits, potentially replacing the battery packs currently used to power electronic components.
“We expect the first iteration to appear as solar energy blocks for use in the SparkBlocks portfolio in children’s educational kits, replacing the battery packs in the current kits, on relatively short terms,” Van Best said.
Once the researchers have gained more experience with manufacturing and performance, they plan to explore scaling the technology to architectural brick-like dimensions. Such developments could eventually support the integration of colourful solar-harvesting elements into buildings and public infrastructure, although no commercial deployment timetable has been established.
“The eventual application and integration of LSC systems will be best initiated by a creative artistic mind, and I look forward to see what such creative persons will come up with,” Van Best concluded.
Luminescent solar concentrators have been investigated for a range of applications, including
solar windows
agrivoltaic systems and greenhouses
bifacial PV installations
. Researchers from the University of Twente found that free-space LSCs could increase winter electricity generation by up to 60% and annual energy yield by 12% compared with conventional monofacial systems.
Researchers at Eindhoven University of Technology have also explored LSC technology in previous studies. In
, a TU/e research team developed measurement protocols to standardize the characterization of LSC devices and support their commercial development. In
, a Dutch-Australian research group involving TU/e scientists developed cubical LSC devices equipped with bifacial silicon solar cells for urban applications, with the best-performing configuration achieving a power conversion efficiency of 11.6%.

title: Satellite imagery reveals vegetation recovery at solar plant in semi-arid region of China - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Satellite imagery of a 21 GW solar power complex in China’s Qinghai province shows that vegetation recovered within two years of PV installation. The researchers found that vegetation density increased by an average of 28.4% in the second to fifth years after construction, compared with pre-construction levels.
Emiliano Bellini
17 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
Schematic of PV-panel mask extraction
Researchers at China’s Hohai University have examined seasonal vegetation changes at the
21 GW Gonghe Talatan solar power cluster
in Gonghe County, Hainan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, Qinghai province, China, and have found that vegetation levels surpassed pre-construction levels within two years of PV installation.
The region is characterized by predominantly flat terrain at an average elevation of approximately 2,920 meters and a cold, arid to semi-arid climate. Average annual temperatures stand at 4.1 C, while annual precipitation reaches 303 mm, nearly 88% of which falls between May and September. Annual evaporation amounts to approximately 1,800 mm, while the region receives more than 2,900 hours of sunshine per year and experiences significant wind-driven sand movement.
The scientists used a multiscale analytical approach combining high-resolution satellite imagery with long-term satellite observations. They analyzed four Beijing-3 satellite images acquired between May and August 2025, each with a spatial resolution of 1.2 meters. The images enabled them to identify solar panels and assess vegetation growing between them using the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), calculated from red and near-infrared reflectance.
The researchers manually mapped the solar panels to exclude panel-covered areas from the vegetation analysis. They also used Landsat satellite imagery with a spatial resolution of 30 meters to track vegetation changes between 2008 and 2025. The datasets were processed through Google Earth Engine to generate annual maximum NDVI measurements.
To assess vegetation differences, the team compared conditions within the solar plants with those in adjacent control areas extending up to 120 meters beyond the plant boundaries. Areas overlapping with neighboring PV installations were excluded, while only control areas larger than 500 square meters were retained to ensure reliable comparisons.
The researchers also examined monthly vegetation changes from May to August using Landsat imagery covering 2024 to 2026. To minimize interference from solar panels in the lower-resolution Landsat images, they developed a filtering method based on panel coverage. They tested five coverage thresholds ranging from 30% to 70% to assess their influence on NDVI measurements.
For the long-term analysis, they retained pixels with solar panel coverage of 50% or less. Vegetation records were then aligned according to each plant’s construction year, enabling the researchers to examine changes from five years before installation to 10 years afterward. Plants installed in 2021, 2024, and 2025 were excluded from this analysis because of insufficient pre- and post-construction observations.
The analysis of 158 PV plant sites in 2025 showed that vegetation within the installations was consistently greener than in surrounding areas, with average NDVI values within the plants being 11.5% higher than in adjacent control areas, with the largest difference recorded in August.
Landsat observations from 2024 to 2026 confirmed this pattern across all 12 monthly comparisons, with NDVI differences ranging from 3.5% to 10.7%. Long-term satellite data also revealed sustained improvements in vegetation conditions following PV construction.
The researchers found that NDVI exceeded pre-construction levels by 19.9% in the second year after installation and was, on average, 28.4% higher between the second and fifth years. Plants completed between 2013 and 2018 recorded increases ranging from 14.1% to 35.9%, with older installations generally showing stronger vegetation recovery.
“Generally, the NDVI within the PV plant polygons was slightly higher than that in the surrounding external areas,” the researchers explained. “This difference was particularly observed in the southern PV plant polygons, where vegetation greenness was obviously higher than that observed in the other PV plant polygons.”
The researchers suggested that panel shading, reduced evaporation, lower wind speeds and rainfall redistribution could contribute to improved growing conditions. Water from panel cleaning and vegetation reseeding may also play a role, although these mechanisms were not directly verified.
They cautioned that climatic variability, uncertainties associated with satellite measurements and the lack of field observations limit the findings, which may not be directly applicable to regions with different environmental conditions.
Their findings are presented in the study “
Impacts of large-scale centralized photovoltaic plant construction on vegetation: Satellite evidence from Gonghe photovoltaic park, China
,” published in
Information Geography
Previous research has also highlighted the potential environmental benefits of large-scale PV installations in arid regions. In October 2024,
scientists at China’s Xi’an University of Technology
examined the ecological effects of a 1 GW solar installation at the Qinghai Gonghe Photovoltaic Park. They found that the installation achieved a higher environmental assessment score than surrounding areas, suggesting improvements in local microclimate conditions, soil properties, and plant and microbial diversity.
More recently,
researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences
examined the cooling effects of eight solar plants in China’s arid regions. They found that PV installations can create localized cooling effects extending between 120 meters and 540 meters beyond their boundaries, with cooling intensity reaching 3.1 C in some locations. Vegetation responses varied depending on seasonal conditions, geographical location and plant design, suggesting that the ecological benefits of large-scale solar development are strongly site-dependent.

content:
Applications & Installations
Vietnam’s uptake of floating solar projects continues with three provinces progressing utility-scale projects, including a groundbreaking ceremony for a 35 MW array.
Patrick Jowett
17 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Authorities in three Vietnamese provinces have advanced plans for utility-scale floating solar projects, with installations ranging from 30 MW to over 300 MW.
The province of Gai Lai in southcentral Vietnam is preparing a groundbreaking ceremony for a 35 MW floating solar project this week.
The Bau Can floating solar power plant is expected to span 47 hectares in total, 30 of which will cover the surface on the Bau Can lake.
Local press lists Bau Can Solar Energy joint stock company (JSC) as the investor, with total costs expected to reach VND 613 billion ($23.8 million).
Installation is due for completion in July 2028, with commissioning scheduled for a month later. Once completed, the project is expected to supply nearly 59 GWh
annually over a 50 year operating life.
The province of Lam Dong, southern Vietnam, has backed investment in a planned floating solar array to be installed on the Dak Sin 1 hydroelectric reservoir in Quang Ting commune.
The floating PV project has a planned capacity of 30 MW. It will utilise around 33 hectares of land, 31 of which will be on the water surface.
It will be implemented by VRG Dak Nong JSC, with total investment expected to reach VND 499.5 billion. The project is due to be completed and put into operation by the fourth quarter of 2028.
The province of Dak Lak, just south of Gai Lai province, recently granted a 50-year lease for a large-scale floating solar project to be built on the Srepok 3 hydropower reservoir, located across Ea Nuol and Ea Wer communes.
Developer Srepok 3 Solar Power JSC has been given permission to cover 354 hectares of the reservoir with the solar installation.
A letter confirming the approval states the developer has full exemption from land rental payments for the entire 50 year lease period but says it must complete the relevant legal procedures before using the reservoir’s water surface.
The letter does not state a planned capacity for the floating PV project but details on the provincial government of Dak Lak’s website states a proposed capacity of 304 MW, alongside investment of VND 7.661 trillion. It also gives a target commissioning date by the end of 2027.
Earlier this month, authorities in Dak Lak
approved a 452 MW floating solar project
on the Ea Sup Thuong reservoir. The project is scheduled for completion by the end of 2028 and would rank among the world’s largest inland floating PV installations.
The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade recently announced
new regional electricity generation price ceilings
for ground-mounted and floating solar projects. Floating solar projects are subject to higher ceilings than ground-mounting projects, ranging from VND 1,340.21 ($0.052)/kWh in the south to VND 1,939.74/kWh in the north.

title: Camera-based navigation allows US Navy drone to fly 6 hours without GPS
content: The US Navy has tested a camera-based navigation system that allows drones to fly without relying on GPS signals. A ScanEagle unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) completed a six-hour flight over open ocean near Southern California, navigating to designated waypoints using cameras and motion sensors. Developed by California-based Rhoman Aerospace in collaboration with the Naval Postgraduate School, the system was tested in a simulated GPS-denied environment with satellite navigation and ground links switched offAccording to the team, the drone maintained closed-loop flight with less than 0.5 percent position drift relative to the distance traveled.GPS-free drone navigationThe new technology combines visual-inertial odometry (VIO), onboard cameras, motion sensors, and flight telemetry to estimate an aircraft’s position and movement.The system was tested aboard a ScanEagle drone near San Clemente Island, off Southern California, where it completed a six-hour flight with satellite navigation and ground communication links disabled. The trials demonstrated how sensor fusion and onboard autonomy could help drones maintain their flight paths in environments where GPS signals are jammed, spoofed, or unavailable.Conventional visual navigation systems work by identifying recognizable features in the terrain below an aircraft and using them as reference points to calculate its geographical position. Cameras continuously capture images of the surrounding environment, while image-processing algorithms identify and track distinct visual features. These observations are combined with information from inertial sensors, including accelerometers and gyroscopes, which measure changes in the aircraft’s movement and orientation. With visual position estimates, and motion measurements, the system can calculate its trajectory without receiving satellite navigation signals.Smarter maritime navigationResearchers noted that applying the conventional approach over open water presents a different technical challenge. Unlike land environments, oceans lack permanent visual landmarks that cameras can reliably identify and track. Waves, changing light conditions, and the constantly moving water surface make it difficult for conventional visual-inertial odometry algorithms to establish consistent reference points. To address this problem, Rhoman adapted its VIO technology with sensor-fusion methods designed specifically for maritime environments. The system combines camera observations with onboard sensor measurements and aircraft telemetry to generate navigation estimates. It can also operate with or without preloaded terrain maps.The navigation technology pairs with the Naval Postgraduate School’s CAVR autonomy architecture to provide onboard flight control. This system processes data from the sensor-fusion setup to keep the aircraft on its assigned path. When GPS signals or ground communications drop out, the architecture automatically takes over to ensure the drone completes its mission without needing continuous commands from a remote operator.During the trials near San Clemente Island, the ScanEagle flew several miles offshore and followed flight profiles involving different patterns and altitudes. Researchers simulated the loss of satellite navigation and ground communication links to evaluate the system’s ability to maintain autonomous flight. The aircraft completed six hours of operations and successfully reached its designated waypoints. The reported navigation drift remained below 0.5 percent of the distance flown.According to the team, the technology is designed to be platform-agnostic rather than limited to the ScanEagle. The next development phase will integrate it with AeroVironment’s JUMP 20 vertical takeoff and landing UAV. Future testing will expand the aircraft’s flight envelope and examine how atmospheric conditions and changes in the ocean surface affect navigation performance.Researchers note that by combining camera-based positioning, inertial sensing, and onboard autonomy, the system could provide UAVs with an alternative navigation method in GPS-denied environments.

title: Lotus-stem bio-generator produces continuous electricity for 30 days
content: Researchers in China have designed a bio-hybrid micro-generator that can produce continuous low-voltage electricity for more than 30 days by combining natural lotus stems with electroactive bacteria. The system uses water transport and ambient evaporation, eliminating the need for moving parts, external power, or fossil fuels.Hydrovoltaic energy harvesting, which generates electricity directly from the interaction between water and solid surfaces, has long attracted interest as a clean power source for remote electronics. However, maintaining steady electrical output over extended periods has remained a persistent challenge due to sluggish fluid transport and unstable charge separation. To solve this, the research team turned to the natural vascular architecture of lotus stems, which are evolved to efficiently pull water upward from roots to leaves.lotus-stem hydrovoltaic generators. Journal CellHow the bio-hybrid generator worksAs detailed in the journal Device and reported by the South China Morning Post (SCMP), the fabrication process begins by submerging sections of lotus stems in a culture of Geobacter sulfurreducens. It is a species of electroactive bacterium known for its ability to transfer electrons through conductive protein filaments.Over a 24-hour immersion period, the microorganisms colonized the interior walls of the stems’ vertical, porous microchannels. The researchers then freeze-dried the colonized stems to preserve their structural integrity and attached titanium mesh electrodes to both the top and bottom ends.When the bottom of the treated stem is placed in water, natural capillary action draws liquid upward through the aligned channels. As water reaches the top and evaporates into the surrounding air, it drives a continuous upward flow of charged ions. The bacterial biofilm lining the channels interacts with this moving fluid, facilitating charge separation. Positively charged ions accumulate near the upper titanium electrode, creating a steady electrical potential difference between the top and bottom of the stem that produces a continuous, low-voltage current.Scaling up from calculators to smartphonesIn laboratory testing, a single lotus-stem generator sustained stable power generation for more than 30 days. While an individual unit produces only a small voltage, the researchers demonstrated that multiple units can be wired together to meet practical power demands. Connecting three generators in series produced enough energy to run a pocket calculator, while six units successfully powered a small lamp and an electronic ink display.To test higher-demand electronics, the team assembled a 16-by-16 grid containing 256 individual lotus-stem generators. Paired with a voltage converter, the array generated enough power to run a mobile phone. According to the researchers, this modular scalability makes the hydrovoltaic technology particularly promising for low-maintenance, distributed sensor networks and off-grid environmental monitors deployed near rivers, lakes, or agricultural wetlands.Engineering hurdles before commercializationDespite the encouraging 30-day endurance run, the study authors noted that significant manufacturing hurdles stand between the laboratory prototype and commercial deployment. As natural lotus stems vary in diameter, pore distribution, and structural density, achieving uniform electrical output across large batches is difficult. Cultivating consistent Geobacter sulfurreducens biofilms inside biological tissue also adds processing time and material costs.Rather than harvesting wild plants at an industrial scale, the researchers plan to use the lotus stem as a structural blueprint. Up next, the team aims to fabricate synthetic materials with uniform, aligned microchannels that replicate the lotus plant’s fluid-transport efficiency for standardized mass production.

title: US Army seeks oxygen system for 7-hour tiltrotor flights at 18,000 feet
content: The US Army is looking for a portable oxygen system that can keep three crew members supplied for about seven hours aboard its new MV-75 Cheyenne II tiltrotor. In a market survey posted on November 16, the service asked companies for a unit that can generate oxygen aboard the aircraft during flights at altitudes of up to 18,000 feet.The Army wants crews to be able to install the system before a long flight and remove it afterward. Generating oxygen in flight would also reduce reliance on cylinders that need refilling on the ground, a consideration for an aircraft intended to operate from remote locations.A suitcase-sized unit for three crew membersThe notice calls for enough oxygen to supply “a minimum of two pilots and one nonrated crewmember for approximately seven hours.” It describes a “roll-on/roll-off” unit that would fit in a space about 24 centimeters wide, 40 centimeters deep and 70 centimeters tall, roughly the size of an upright carry-on suitcase.Fitting the unit into that space is only part of the requirement. The Army said it must also leave room for crews to exit in an emergency and reach their survival equipment. The notice addresses oxygen for the flight crew. It gives no requirements for soldiers riding in the back.Why the Army is planning seven-hour flightsThe MV-75 is designed to take off and land vertically like a helicopter. Once airborne, it can tilt its rotors forward and fly like an airplane. The Army expects it to fly about twice as fast and twice as far as the Black Hawk helicopters it will partly replace.That range is central to what the Army calls “self-deployment,” in which the aircraft flies to its destination under its own power. The service specified a one-way range of roughly 2,800 miles without refueling. At the MV-75’s planned cruising speed of 280 knots, seven hours in the air would cover about 2,250 miles. The oxygen survey describes how long the equipment would need to supply the crew on such flights.Bell completes the first fuselageThe oxygen survey appeared on the same day Bell said it had completed the first MV-75 fuselage and sent it to Texas for final assembly. The fuselage milestone comes seven months after the Army named the aircraft Cheyenne II in April.Companies have until December 16 to respond to the survey. The notice gives suppliers an opportunity to describe equipment that could meet the Army’s needs. It lists no purchase quantity, price, or date by which the equipment would be needed. Any contract would be a separate step. The Army said it wants more flexibility to fly from places where oxygen support “may be limited or unavailable.” A system that makes oxygen aboard the aircraft would let crews start another flight from those locations without first finding a facility equipped to refill cylinders.

title: 20,000-ton plant recovers 90% of key metals from spent EV batteries
content: After years of shipping valuable battery waste abroad and paying a steep strategic price to buy back the refined metals, Europe is reclaiming its supply chain.French environmental giant Veolia has launched a battery recycling facility in France’s Grand Est region to keep valuable raw materials on European soil. “For too long, Europe has watched its strategic raw materials leave the continent, only to import finished products from elsewhere,” said Stéphane Séjourné, Executive Vice President of the European Commission.“We must break free from this cycle of dependency. This new plant in the Grand Est region is ‘Made in Europe’ in action: resources recycled in Europe, processed in Europe, to power our batteries in Europe.”Securing critical metalsElectric vehicle batteries contain plastics, solvents, and critical metals like lithium, cobalt, copper, manganese, and nickel. Mining these scarce minerals is geographically concentrated, which often creates supply tensions. The new site will look into dark, granular powder known as “black mass,” the shredded remains of spent batteries. Currently, intense foreign competition drives massive exports of this material to Asia for processing. Veolia’s facility uses proprietary hydrometallurgy technology to interrupt that outflow, extracting more than 90 percent of the cobalt, nickel, and copper trapped inside the powder.Conventional smelting, known as pyrometallurgy, demands extreme heat, consumes massive amounts of energy, and yields lower-purity metals. Veolia’s chemical-based process operates at far lower temperatures and uses much less power. This gentle approach extracts battery-grade minerals ready for immediate reuse in European manufacturing.The goals set in numbers is huge. Each year, the plant will process roughly 7,000 tonnes of black mass sourced from France, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland. That volume equals about 20,000 tonnes of spent batteries. Once purified, the metals will feed directly back into Europe’s automotive, construction, and defense sectors.All these efforts are important for the continent’s green transition. Within the next five years, nearly 700,000 tonnes of batteries are projected to reach the end of their life across Europe. Those spent units hold more than one billion euros in recoverable strategic metals. Capturing that value locally is seen as essential for establishing a true “battery-to-battery” manufacturing loop.Europe’s battery mandateRecycling spent batteries prevents toxic pollution, reduces carbon emissions, and eases pressure on raw material extraction. To enforce this shift, European legislators introduced strict rules requiring new batteries to include recycled metals, reaching 26% cobalt, 15% nickel, and 12% lithium by 2036. These regulations also mandate recycling recovery rates of 95% for cobalt, copper, and nickel, alongside 80% for lithium by 2031.The French facility acts as the downstream anchor for a wider continental network. Veolia is simultaneously deploying upstream battery-dismantling projects across the United Kingdom, Belgium, and Slovenia to ensure a steady pipeline of feedstock.Regional leaders view the investment as both an economic engine and a strategic shield. Franck Leroy, President of the Grand Est Region, praised the facility as an industrial showcase that proves local partnerships can build a circular economy while reinforcing European energy sovereignty.Industry analysts and policymakers agree that technology alone will not secure the supply chain. Sustained public backing and strict regulatory frameworks, including the EU Battery Regulation and the upcoming Circular Economy Act, remain vital to ensure recycled metals are reintegrated into European factories rather than lost to global competitors.

title: Meet Howl: Humanoid robot learning to collect eggs from poultry farms
content: Humanoid robots are taking on an unusual new chore: collecting eggs from poultry farms. Researchers at North Carolina State University are developing Howl, a four-foot-tall robot that detects and picks up eggs laid on the floors of cage-free poultry houses. The project, which uses Unitree G1 robots as a base, aims to address labor shortages while improving bird welfare and productivity. The egg-collecting robot is part of a broader effort by the university’s Artificial Intelligence & Robotics Lab to bring advanced automation to commercial poultry farming.AI-powered egg harvesterThe four-foot-tall robot called Howl, which is basically a Unitree G1 humanoid, detects and retrieves eggs laid outside nesting boxes in cage-free poultry houses. The project is part of a broader effort to use automation, machine learning and computer vision to address labor shortages, reduce egg losses and improve animal welfare.The shift toward cage-free egg production has created new challenges for poultry farmers. Unlike conventional cage systems, where eggs roll onto conveyor belts for collection, cage-free barns require some eggs to be gathered manually from the floor. In some environments, these floor eggs can account for 2 percent to 15 percent of total production.Members of the AIR Lab are working to code Howl’s movements so the robot can pick up floor eggs.For a farm housing around 100,000 birds, that could mean as many as 15,000 eggs requiring collection each day. The process is labor-intensive, and delays in retrieving eggs can affect product quality. Howl is being developed to automate this task using artificial intelligence and robotic manipulation. The robot is designed to identify eggs on the floor, approach them, and pick them up using its robotic hands.Training the humanoid to perform these movements requires developing its control and response systems largely from scratch. Researchers are using virtual reality (VR) manipulation to demonstrate tasks and program robotic movements. The training also incorporates machine learning techniques, including reinforcement learning and imitation learning, to help the robot learn how to handle eggs.The team is currently refining Howl’s programming and training, with egg-detection and retrieval simulations expected to be completed before moving toward practical demonstrations. The researchers aim to have the robot performing these tasks by early 2027.Smarter poultry farmingBeyond robotic egg collection, the university is developing AI tools to help poultry producers make better use of farm data and scientific information.One project, called Poultry Talk, is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) platform designed to function as a specialized AI assistant for the poultry industry. It combines a large language model with a curated database of poultry science documents, including peer-reviewed research and publicly available agricultural extension publications.Users can ask questions about subjects such as poultry nutrition, disease diagnosis and prevention, housing, animal welfare, production management and precision farming. Rather than relying on generic internet information, the system retrieves relevant material from its specialized knowledge base to generate more focused responses. The platform has a working demonstration that is being shared with poultry professionals for feedback and further development.Another project focuses on monitoring the health of individual birds using computer vision and AI. Researchers are installing fixed two-dimensional and three-dimensional cameras inside a poultry research facility, where computer vision models analyze individual birds and assess their physical condition.The system evaluates characteristics such as feather condition, plumage density, and body weight to generate individual health assessments. By tracking these indicators, the technology aims to identify early signs of disease or stress that might otherwise go unnoticed in large flocks.The collected data could also support precision feeding systems, allowing farmers to adjust diets and management conditions according to individual birds’ needs rather than treating an entire flock as a uniform population.Together, the projects demonstrate how humanoid robotics, computer vision and specialized AI platforms could bring more automation and data-driven decision-making to poultry production. The longer-term goal is to reduce dependence on manual labor while improving egg collection, flock monitoring and the efficiency of commercial farming operations.

title: NVIDIA speeds up cell analysis 900x, cuts black-hole data to 8 minutes
content: NVIDIA is combining open models designed for scientific research with expanded GPU-accelerated computing libraries to help researchers analyze complex data, run simulations, and speed up discoveries across fields ranging from astrophysics to drug development.The company introduced NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, a package built around its Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model, a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes. It also expanded its CUDA-X libraries with tools for scientific workloads, including black-hole imaging, molecular simulations, materials research and single-cell biology.The developments aim to help researchers build specialized agents that can reason through scientific problems and use computational tools to carry out research tasks.New tools target research bottlenecksA key addition is LitmusBench v0.2, an open dataset containing nearly 50,000 questions for training and evaluating models on chemistry reasoning. Drawing on molecular properties and experimental drug-discovery data, it helps researchers improve predictions of molecular behavior, including solubility and how the human body processes compounds.NVIDIA’s CUDA-X expansion targets the computing bottlenecks that can slow down scientific work. Its cuPhoton toolkit, for example, includes modules that accelerate the processing of astronomical observations.Using cuPhoton.xBeam, researchers can correlate data from the Event Horizon Telescope in eight minutes, compared with more than a month previously, NVIDIA said. The telescope links radio dishes around the world to create an Earth-sized observing instrument, generating petabytes of data that require extensive processing.The company also highlighted work with Pacific Fusion, whose researchers used the cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations were running. Coupled with a locally running Nemotron-powered agent, the workflow could help researchers analyze results and steer simulations in real time.From molecules to biologyIn drug discovery, NVIDIA’s cuPotential accelerates molecular simulation software by up to three times while improving calculation stability and accuracy. The technology can help researchers investigate molecular binding sites and interactions before committing to costly laboratory experiments.NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and several molecular simulation software communities to bring the acceleration to existing workflows. Drug discovery companies including Terray Therapeutics, Topos Bio and Genesis Molecular AI are adopting the technology.For materials research, Daviator GPU kernels for the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package are coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI. They can accelerate quantum-mechanical calculations by up to 22 times while reducing costs by as much as 75%, according to NVIDIA.The expanded toolkit also includes cuSpa, which accelerates cell polygon calculations. At Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, it enabled the generation of large spatial graphs with a reported 900-fold speedup over CPUs.Researchers adapt open modelsResearch organizations and life sciences companies are also adapting Nemotron for specialized scientific tasks.Terray Therapeutics used post-training to extract chemical reactions and conditions from scientific diagrams, while Lila Sciences applied the model to laboratory protocols and quantum-dot production. Therna used it for agent-based mRNA therapeutic design.Argonne National Laboratory is integrating Nemotron into its StructBioReasoner multi-agent system to design and evaluate protein-based therapeutic candidates.Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and LitmusBench v0.2 are available on Hugging Face. NVIDIA has also optimized the model to run locally on its 128GB DGX Spark system, giving researchers an option to work on infrastructure they control.Together, the model and computing tools are intended to help scientists move from interpreting research data to running more complex computational experiments and developing specialized scientific workflows.

title: Autonomous cargo eVTOL carries 550 pounds without a runway or pilot
content: An autonomous electric aircraft designed to move heavy cargo is heading to the United States for flight demonstrations. The AIR 120D can carry approximately 550 pounds without requiring a conventional runway or an onboard pilot.AIR has shipped its first AIR 120D cargo aircraft to its Florida headquarters. The aircraft will undergo flight demonstrations as the aerospace manufacturer expands its operations in the US. Its arrival also advances plans to establish domestic production and flight operations.The aircraft targets logistics missions where conventional transportation infrastructure presents limitations. Its combination of vertical flight and autonomous operation could make remote resupply more practical. Military logistics also represents a potential application for the platform.Cargo aircraft without runwaysThe AIR 120D uses electric propulsion and vertical takeoff and landing capabilities. It can operate without the long, prepared surfaces that conventional cargo aircraft require. That makes it suitable for locations with limited aviation infrastructure. View this post on Instagram Its cargo bay provides approximately 70 cubic feet of storage space. The aircraft can accommodate payloads weighing up to 550 pounds. That capacity opens possibilities beyond lightweight package deliveries.Potential missions include remote resupply, maritime logistics, and humanitarian assistance. Commercial operators could also use the aircraft for mid-mile cargo transportation. Its autonomous flight system removes the need for an onboard pilot.The US Department of War classifies the AIR 120D within its Group 4 uncrewed aircraft systems category. This classification places the aircraft among larger military drone platforms. AIR designed it to address transportation challenges in contested and infrastructure-limited environments.Engineering for autonomous cargoDeveloping an aircraft capable of carrying substantial payloads requires more than vertical flight. Its propulsion system must generate sufficient lift throughout takeoff, flight, and landing. Battery performance also influences payload capacity and operational range.AIR says its cargo program has accumulated more than two years of development experience. Earlier aircraft provided hundreds of development flights and valuable customer feedback. Engineers used those findings to refine propulsion, battery systems, avionics, and autonomous flight capabilities.The company first flew its production cargo configuration in April 2026. The latest shipment brings that development program to the US. Demonstrations at its Florida headquarters will help advance its operational plans.AIR CEO and co-founder Rani Plaut pointed to Florida’s investment in advanced aviation infrastructure. He said the aircraft’s arrival would help demonstrate autonomous cargo transportation. Plaut also cited the platform’s ability to carry substantial payloads into difficult-to-reach locations.Florida becomes production hubAIR’s expansion in Florida involves more than its cargo aircraft. The manufacturer announced a partnership involving its Florida headquarters in August. Its plans include flight programs for the AIR ONE personal eVTOL.The state has also partnered with AIR through the Florida Department of Transportation. That relationship supports infrastructure development for advanced air mobility operations. Establishing production and flight activities could strengthen Florida’s position in emerging aviation technologies.The AIR 120D demonstrations will provide another opportunity to evaluate autonomous cargo operations. Repeatable flights and production capabilities remain important steps toward wider deployment. Military and commercial logistics operators could eventually benefit from aircraft that transport heavy supplies without traditional runway infrastructure.

title: NVIDIA develops quantum error-correction decoder with 13,000x speedup
content: NVIDIA has introduced a new quantum error-correction decoding algorithm that it says can accelerate research workloads by up to 13,000 times, potentially helping scientists investigate designs for more practical fault-tolerant quantum computers.The TCBP-JOBS algorithm, available through the NVIDIA CUDA-Q QEC 0.9.0 library, reduces the computation time for studying new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to just 45 minutes, according to the company.The development comes as NVIDIA expands its quantum-computing collaboration with IBM and the US Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab). The three organizations also plan to establish a modular quantum-computing codesign platform to investigate how quantum processors and conventional computing systems can work together.Faster decoding tackles errorsQuantum processors are vulnerable to errors that can limit the complexity and duration of computations. Unlike conventional bits, quantum bits, or qubits, can exist in combinations of states, making them particularly sensitive to disturbances.Quantum error correction protects information by distributing it across multiple physical qubits. A classical computing algorithm called a decoder then analyses measurement data to identify likely errors so they can be corrected.NVIDIA’s TCBP-JOBS algorithm accelerates this decoding process for research workloads. The company says it delivers up to 13,000 times faster decoding than existing leading algorithms while maintaining high accuracy.Faster decoding could allow researchers to test different error-correction codes and decoder configurations more efficiently. It may also help scientists identify designs that use physical qubits more effectively, an important consideration as researchers work towards fault-tolerant quantum systems.The algorithm is designed to accelerate research rather than demonstrate that quantum processors have already achieved fault-tolerant operation.Quantum joins supercomputing workflowsSeparately, IBM, NVIDIA and Fermilab plan to develop a modular quantum-computing codesign platform by colocating NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by its Nighthawk processor.The platform will allow researchers to investigate error-correction codes, decoding algorithms, and quantum-classical applications. Fermilab will contribute expertise in high-energy and nuclear physics, helping researchers explore scientific problems that could benefit from future quantum systems.The collaboration also aims to examine how classical computing resources can scale alongside multiple interconnected quantum processors.Another part of the effort focuses on integrating quantum processors into supercomputing workflows. NVIDIA is expanding the open-source Slurm workload manager with a quantum interface, while IBM is contributing through its Quantum Resource Management Interface.Slurm already helps supercomputing centers allocate computing resources, including CPUs and GPUs. The new capabilities are intended to let researchers schedule quantum processors using familiar commands and resource-management policies, without maintaining separate workflows.IBM, RIKEN and NVIDIA are also exploring quantum-classical computing for scientific simulations. In separate research involving an iron-sulfur cluster found in proteins, the team reported a 79-fold improvement in accuracy over earlier runs of the same experiment.The researchers used circuits involving up to 72 qubits and 4,000 two-qubit operations, combining quantum processing with NVIDIA GPU-accelerated calculations. The results came within 4.3 millihartree of the accuracy achieved using density-matrix renormalization group, a leading classical simulation method.Together, the developments highlight efforts to combine quantum processors with accelerated classical computing, addressing challenges in error correction, system integration and scientific applications.

title: Lux supercomputer enters world's top 15 to power US Genesis Mission
content: A new supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) has entered the world’s top 15, delivering 220.79 petaflops as it opens to scientific users supporting the US Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission.Named Lux, the system ranked No. 14 on the latest TOP500 list, which tracks the world’s most powerful supercomputers. Its debut marks the first major addition to DOE’s computing infrastructure dedicated to the Genesis Mission, a national initiative to accelerate scientific discovery by combining Super Intelligence (SI), high-performance computing (HPC), quantum systems and advanced scientific instruments.Lux was developed through a public-private partnership involving ORNL, AMD and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE). The system pairs AMD Instinct MI355X graphics processing units (GPUs) with AMD EPYC central processing units, Pensando networking and ROCm software. HPE built the system using its ProLiant Compute XD685 platform.The combination is designed to bring SI workloads closer to traditional scientific modeling and simulation. Researchers can use the system to train and run models, process experimental data and coordinate complex workflows, including those involving autonomous agents.A hybrid computing architectureLux supports both Slurm and Kubernetes for resource scheduling, combining established practices from supercomputing with tools commonly used in cloud environments. The arrangement is intended to let researchers run HPC simulations alongside SI training, inference, and agentic workflow orchestration.The system is part of DOE’s Genesis Mission, which aims to build an integrated science discovery platform connecting government, industry, academia and philanthropy. Its first phase targets challenges in energy, scientific discovery and national security.About half of Lux’s annual 3.5 million node-hours will be allocated to Genesis Mission projects. The remaining capacity will be available to AMD under the partnership, allowing the company to develop its SI and HPC technologies, software ecosystem and workloads.Research targets span disciplinesProjects allocated to Lux include work on SI-assisted fusion power plant design, materials development and advanced manufacturing, and Earth system prediction.The fusion project aims to develop an SI platform integrating HPC tools with robotic system design. A separate materials initiative will create a “foundation model factory” to develop customized models that US industry can use. Another project will forecast water availability, streamflow, and river temperatures weeks to years ahead in the Tennessee Valley Authority region, with potential applications for hydropower and thermoelectric operations.ORNL is leading six other Genesis Mission projects and participating in 30 more led by national laboratories, universities and industry partners. The laboratory is also spearheading the American Science Cloud, a secure platform intended to connect computing, data and experimental resources across the DOE’s 17 national laboratories.Lux joins ORNL’s Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility alongside Frontier, the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier. DOE’s next flagship system, Discovery, is scheduled for delivery in 2028.The launch extends a long-running collaboration between the national laboratory and industry, while giving researchers additional computing capacity to combine modeling, simulation, and data-driven methods. Its TOP500 debut places it among the leading systems available for scientific workloads.
