title: US' uncrewed warfare capabilities to get boost with new robotic vehicle
content: The U.S. Marine Corps is set to get increased uncrewed warfare capabilities. The U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory (MCWL) in Quantico is now acquiring two RIPSAW M3 robotic ground vehicles from Textron Systems and its subsidiary, Howe & Howe. Rather than serving as conventional operational vehicles, the platforms will initially function as experimentation and integration testbeds, allowing Marines to evaluate different payloads, sensors and mission configurations.Robotic ground vehicles set the bar for speed, agility“Textron Systems’ M3 robotic ground vehicles set the bar for speed, agility and multi-mission flexibility,” said Vice President of Programs, Sara Willett. “Pairing the M3’s proven capability and reliability with the MCWL mission to drive future operational concepts and capabilities will enable the Marine Corps to advance uncrewed force design and battlefield utility.”Textron revealed that the M3 vehicles will serve as experimentation and integration testbeds, providing Marines the opportunity to integrate various payloads and sensors, demonstrate mission sets and inform additional robotics requirements.M3 robotic vehicle incorporates modular open systems architectureLeveraging Textron Systems’ more than sixty years of experience in multidomain uncrewed technologies for air, land and sea, the M3 vehicle incorporates modular open systems architecture (MOSA) to provide the warfighter with increased agility and functionality in even the most complex battlefield environments. The vehicle offers more than 5,000 pounds of payload capacity, a flat deck to support a variety of payloads, and operational speeds in excess of 30 miles per hour to support missions in complex terrains across the globe, according to a press release.“For over two decades, Howe and Howe, Inc. has been developing highly capable off-road multi-domain platforms where consideration for extreme use and durability have been paramount design characteristics,” said Senior Vice President, Michael Howe. “The M3 will be a great fit for the Marine Corps and its demanding environmental requirements. Howe and Howe Inc. is not only proud to deliver the RIPSAW M3 vehicle but also pleased to work closely with the Marine Corps to develop technologies that fit their specific needs well into the future.”With more than three million operational hours of uncrewed experience across air, land and sea domains, Textron Systems claims that it continues to expand its autonomous technology to support current and future mission sets. The acquisition reflects the growing importance of robotic and autonomous technologies in modern warfare. Militaries worldwide are increasingly exploring uncrewed systems to improve operational flexibility, reduce risks to personnel and expand their ability to conduct missions in challenging environments.Through the RIPSAW M3 programme, the Marine Corps will have an opportunity to experiment with different robotic capabilities and assess how uncrewed ground vehicles can support its evolving operational requirements.The vehicles will enable Marines to integrate various mission payloads and sensors, demonstrate potential mission applications and identify additional requirements for future robotic systems. The findings from these activities are expected to help inform the Marine Corps’ broader approach to uncrewed force design and battlefield integration.By using the RIPSAW M3 as a test platform, the Marine Corps can evaluate how different payloads and sensor systems perform in various mission scenarios. This will help identify practical applications for robotic ground vehicles and provide insights into the technologies required for their future integration.

title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures, 418 flights delayed
content: United Airlines has restored its systems following a widespread technology outage that disrupted departing flights across its network on Monday afternoon. The Chicago-based carrier confirmed that its systems were back up after the issue delayed hundreds of flights, although some services continued to experience delays. United also said there was no indication that the incident was related to a cybersecurity issue.In a statement, United confirmed that the outage was limited to departing flights and did not affect aircraft already in the air or services operated by its United Express regional network. The airline apologized to affected customers and said its teams were working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible.Flight-tracking website FlightAware showed 418 delayed United flights late Monday afternoon. Passengers also took to social media to report delays and disruptions at airports. A recording shared through the ATC app captured a United pilot in Houston asking air traffic control for permission to remain at the gate until the airline’s systems were operational again.The airline advised travelers to monitor their flight status through its mobile app or website and check with United before heading to the airport.United resolves outageIn a statement confirming the resolution, United said it had fixed the technology issue that delayed flight departures. The airline reiterated that flights already in progress and services operated by United Express were unaffected, adding that there was no indication the outage was related to a cybersecurity incident.Earlier today we experienced a technology-related issue that impacted some departing flights. The issue has been resolved.Please check the latest status of your flight at https://t.co/BqzX0dcUna or the United app.— United Airlines (@united) November 16, 2026According to an internal memo from United’s pilots’ union seen by Reuters, the company-wide web-based outage affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. The memo said United was unable to provide final aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.Series of major technology disruptionsThe United Airlines outage is the latest in a series of major technology disruptions affecting critical services across the United States in recent days. On Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulties accessing their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused delays in banking services and transactions involving other financial institutions. JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers. Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those…— Chase (@Chase) November 16, 2026Chase attributed the problem to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system and said it was not related to a cyberattack. Customers of other banks, including Bank of America and Wells Fargo, also reported difficulties, while some Zelle transactions experienced delays.On Friday, a malfunctioning router overwhelmed the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control system, prompting a nationwide ground stop that temporarily halted departing flights across the country. The separate incidents have disrupted services spanning aviation, banking, and workplace technology, although there is no indication that the outages are connected.

title: Cold War-era 1,300-mph jets to test advanced hypersonic interceptor
content: Starfighters Space plans to turn its fleet of Cold War-era fighter jets into an airborne testing platform for a new hypersonic interceptor. The Florida-based company has signed an agreement with aerospace developer Horizon Apogee to conduct a series of flight tests in 2027.The campaign will use Starfighters’ F-104 aircraft to carry Horizon Apogee’s Reaver hypersonic interceptor. Engineers will examine how the vehicle performs during flight before attempting a series of drop tests. The work will also help evaluate Orthrus, the propulsion system designed for the interceptor.Horizon Apogee is developing Reaver through the US Army’s xTech|Search 10 competition. The proposed campaign could provide valuable flight data before the program advances toward powered flight testing.F-104 jets take flightThe F-104 Starfighter originally entered service as a supersonic interceptor during the Cold War. Lockheed developed the aircraft, which became known for its slender fuselage and distinctive wing design. Starfighters Space now operates a commercial fleet of these aircraft for specialized flight-testing work.Under the proposed arrangement, an F-104 will carry Reaver beneath its wing. This configuration will let engineers examine how the interceptor interacts with its carrier aircraft during flight. It will also provide an opportunity to assess aerodynamic integration before releasing the vehicle.The Missile with a Man in ItThat became the F-104's nickname after it first flew in 1954. A long, slender fuselage and tiny wings made it look more like a rocket than a fighter. Today, Starfighters Space puts that design to work for aerospace testing. pic.twitter.com/kGC1SUwrf5— Starfighters Space Inc (@StarfightersInc) November 6, 2026The two companies have outlined a five-phase testing campaign in a non-binding memorandum of understanding. Initial work will cover aerodynamic analysis and aircraft fit checks. Flight-readiness preparations will follow before the companies begin airborne evaluations.Starfighters expects captive-carry flights during the second quarter of 2027. Drop tests could follow in the third quarter, subject to the final agreement. The companies still need to establish pricing and other commercial terms.Starfighters CEO Tim Franta said its Mach 2-plus fleet could support advanced aerospace and defense development. He added that real-world flight conditions can help engineers identify technical risks before advancing their hardware.Testing Reaver’s propulsionReaver hypersonic interceptor will use Horizon Apogee’s Orthrus propulsion system, which follows a combined-cycle air-breathing architecture. The design aims to transition between ramjet and scramjet operation as the vehicle accelerates.Ramjets and scramjets both rely on incoming airflow to support combustion. However, they handle that airflow differently. A ramjet slows incoming air to subsonic speeds before combustion, while a scramjet maintains supersonic airflow through its combustion chamber.The transition between these operating modes presents significant engineering challenges. Testing Reaver under different flight conditions could help engineers understand how its airframe and propulsion architecture perform together.Horizon Apogee plans to conduct an earlier vertical launch test of a Reaver prototype in early 2027. The company has selected the US Army’s White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico for that test.CEO Jason Kenney said the F-104 campaign will provide flight data needed to address integration risks. The company previously conducted a subscale hot-fire test in June.The proposed campaign will initially focus on unpowered flight evaluations. Its final phase will involve analyzing collected flight data and considering further testing. Those activities could eventually include powered flight trials.

title: OpenAI agents enter US healthcare after 99% clinical safety rating
content: OpenAI is expanding its computer-use technology into healthcare, allowing AI agents to navigate clinical software and handle repetitive administrative tasks. The technology can retrieve patient information, prepare medical documentation, and coordinate insurance authorization requests across separate applications.The development targets a persistent challenge in U.S. healthcare, where staff often spend considerable time moving information between disconnected systems. OpenAI is working with major healthcare organizations to automate workflows involving referrals, discharge planning, and patient outreach. The goal is to reduce administrative workloads without removing clinicians from important decisions.Agents navigate clinical softwareAn OpenAI demonstration shows how an agent could help process an MRI request for a patient experiencing lower back pain. It starts by reviewing the patient’s electronic health record (EHR), including previous consultations, physical therapy records, and imaging history.The agent then drafts an MRI order, a clinical note, and a response to the patient. Afterward, it uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request through an insurer’s portal. Clinicians and authorization specialists review the documents before taking further action.ChatGPT for Healthcare is advancing with more capable computer-use agents, stronger clinical answers, and 20+ new healthcare plugins.@AbridgeHQ, @AmbienceHealth, @Cigna, @CVSHealth, and other leading healthcare organizations are putting our models to work across prior… pic.twitter.com/zdUatPPG5e— OpenAI (@OpenAI) November 16, 2026Computer-use agents interact with existing applications through clicks and keyboard inputs. This allows them to navigate software functions that traditional application programming interfaces (APIs) may not fully support. The approach could prove particularly useful in healthcare, where organizations rely on multiple systems that do not always communicate with each other.Healthcare partners deploy agentsOpenAI is working with CVS Health, Cigna Healthcare, Abridge, and Ambience to develop practical healthcare applications. CVS Health uses computer-use agents to send documents, process referrals, and support specialist consultations. One agent cleared a document-sending backlog that had accumulated over several months during a single weekend. Another handles software-related steps for tens of thousands of consultations daily.The company also uses validation checks and human oversight to verify agent activity. Its systems capture screenshots and action records, allowing staff to confirm that applications reached the correct states.Cigna Healthcare has introduced the technology to help case managers gather information across more than 10 separate systems. Agents can retrieve details about insurance coverage, providers, appointments, and previous interactions within seconds. This reduces the time staff spend searching through different applications.Abridge is developing agents to coordinate inpatient care, including medication access and home-health arrangements. Ambience, meanwhile, uses computer interaction to prepare insurance authorization requests. Its agent pauses when medical records contain ambiguous information and requests clinician input before proceeding.OpenAI reports safety resultsOpenAI evaluated GPT-6 Astra on clinical tasks involving electronic health record inboxes. Physicians reviewed its actions, documentation, and proposed patient responses to assess their usefulness and potential risks. Of 325 reviewed tasks, 99 percent received a safe rating. Physicians also rated 93 percent of 646 assessments as very or extremely helpful.Administrative performance produced another notable result. On Stanford researchers’ HealthAdminBench, GPT-6 Astra scored 94.3 percent of available points. GPT-6 Luna scored 91.8 percent on the same benchmark. OpenAI also reported a substantial cost difference. Astra completed each benchmark task for approximately 8.5 cents, costing 98 percent less than Luna.Healthcare organizations can access computer-use capabilities through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. They can configure approval requirements, restrict agent permissions, and maintain audit logs to support HIPAA-compliant deployments.

title: JPMorgan Chase glitch delays transactions at major US banks
content: Thousands of customers across U.S. reported difficulty accessing online accounts at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Capital One and US Bank on November 16, after a technical issue at Chase triggered transaction delays across the banking system.Outage-tracking website Downdetector recorded more than 3,300 reports involving Chase by Monday afternoon, while customers also flagged problems at other major financial institutions and the digital payment service Zelle.However, subsequent statements from banks clarified that the disruption was primarily centred on Chase. Bank of America, Citigroup and Capital One said their banking services were operating normally, while US Bank said its systems were not directly affected.Customers reported difficulties logging into banking applications, checking account balances and completing transactions. Some Chase users also received notifications warning that certain services were temporarily unavailable.Chase identifies software bugJPMorgan Chase attributed the disruption to a temporary software bug in its on-premise hardware systems, ruling out a cyberattack.JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers. Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those…— Chase (@Chase) November 16, 2026“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” Joe Evangelisti, a spokesperson for the bank, told the Associated Press.Evangelisti said the issue was limited to Chase and was not indicative of a wider problem affecting the banking sector.“This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.In an earlier statement, Chase said some transactions were taking longer than usual to complete but customers could still access their accounts and funds. The bank added that it was working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.Banks clarify service statusSeveral financial institutions subsequently clarified their positions as reports of widespread outages circulated online.Bank of America and Citigroup said their banking services were not affected by the disruption. Capital One also said its systems were operating normally, despite customer complaints appearing on Downdetector.A spokesperson for US Bank said its systems were not directly affected but warned that customers attempting to send or receive Zelle payments involving another financial institution could experience transaction delays.Zelle’s network operator, Early Warning Services, also said its payment network remained operational. The company explained that technical problems at participating financial institutions could affect the processing of some payments.Zelle is a peer-to-peer payment service that allows customers of participating US banks to transfer money between accounts. Its owners include major financial institutions such as Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.The banking disruption came days after a major Microsoft outage on Thursday, November 12, which affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot for several hours. A separate air traffic control disruption on Friday also grounded flights across the US for several hours. However, no connection between these incidents and the banking problems has been established.The incident highlighted how a technical problem at one major financial institution can affect transactions involving other banks, even when their own banking systems remain operational.

title: Giant 62.5 MW battery could power 21,000 households for four hours
content: German energy giant RWE has just broken ground on a colossal 262.5-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery that is capable of supplying roughly 21,000 households with electricity during peak evening hours.The 62.5-megawatt (MW) battery is reportedly RWE’s first battery energy storage system (BESS) in Italy. Located in the city of Ragusa in Sicily, it will be fitted with 42 containers housing lithium-ion batteries. RWE representatives revealed that the system will have a total storage capacity of 262.5 megawatt-hours (MWh). It will be capable of delivering its maximum output for four hours. This will be enough to cover the evening peak electricity demand of around 21,000 Italian households.The company expects to commission the project by the end of 2027. “The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone,” Sopna Sury, CEO of RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said. “We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun.”Power for peak demandSury explained that the battery will support the balance between electricity supply and demand. “In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilizing the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most,” Sury continued. Unlike conventional power plants, renewable energy sources depend on weather conditions. Battery storage systems can store excess electricity when production is high and release it when the demand increases.RWE said its new battery will provide balancing energy to stabilize the electricity grid. It will also feature technology capable of delivering grid-forming services such as instantaneous reserve, also known as inertia.Apart from installing the batteries, RWE will build the necessary grid infrastructure, including a high-voltage transformer that will link the system to the 150-kilovolt (kV) electricity grid. “[The] Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21.000 households for four hours,” Sury added.More battery capacityWith the project, RWE aims to expand its battery storage business across Europe and other parts of the world. The company currently operates approximately 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage capacity worldwide. At the same time, another three GW are under construction.Additionally, RWE has established a strong presence in Italy’s renewable energy market. It currently operates 18 onshore wind farms, one solar power plant, and three agrivoltaic facilities. Together, these projects have an installed capacity of approximately 670 MW. This is enough to supply renewable electricity to more than 550,000 Italian households.The company is also constructing 200 MW of additional wind and solar capacity across the country. The Ragusa project will complement these renewable energy operations. Meanwhile, RWE plans to develop further battery storage capacity in Italy alongside its existing wind and solar projects.“We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system,” Sury said in a press release. He explained that the expansion will make Italy’s electricity grid more reliable.

title: Q&A: Dr. Dávid Forgács on bringing perovskite PV from the lab to the market with Nexunite
content:
Q&A: Dr. Dávid Forgács on bringing perovskite PV from the lab to the market with Nexunite
Dr. Dávid Forgács has seen perovskite photovoltaics from both sides: the research lab and the company trying to bring the technology to market. He began as a scientist in organic photovoltaics at Fraunhofer ISE, and during his PhD at the University of Valencia he worked on some of the early perovskite tandem devices, building a widely cited research record. He then spent more than seven years at Saule Technologies, one of the first companies working to commercialize perovskite PV. There his work spanned technology and product development, IP management, business development and fundraising, and he even helped bring investment and research-grant funding to the company.
Now he is applying that experience to
Nexunite
, a Budapest-based group he founded and leads as CEO, which aims to bring perovskite PV and other deep-tech innovations out of the lab and into the market. It combines a consulting arm, which supports European R&D funding, consortium building and IP strategy, with an R&D company developing flexible perovskite technology, starting with indoor IoT. Its line is “Flexible Power for Infinite Possibilities.”
We asked him about the idea behind Nexunite, what he sees standing between perovskites and the market, and where he hopes to take the company.
Tell us about your new company, Nexunite.
Nexunite is a Budapest-based group I founded to bring perovskite photovoltaics and other deep-tech innovations from the lab to the market. From the start, I didn’t want it to be just another perovskite startup. I want to build a company that stands on solid ground, with its own revenue from services alongside technology development.
The group has two parts currently:
Nexunite Kft. is the parent company and consulting arm. It covers European R&D funding, consortium building, IP strategy and freedom-to-operate analysis, and techno-economic assessment.
Nexunite Technologies is the R&D company, which owns our IP and is open to investors. We start with indoor IoT, using a flexible perovskite stack made entirely from solution. That’s where we see the low-hanging fruit. Longer term, we plan to address space applications with a different layer stack, along with other niche applications.
What gap did you see in how scientific innovation reaches the market, and why did now feel like the right time to start your company?
Perovskites have reached a turning point. The question is no longer whether they work. High efficiencies are reported routinely and durability keeps improving. What’s left is mainly an engineering problem: reproducible processes, reliable encapsulation, and products that fit a real market. Engineering problems are much more predictable to solve than scientific ones, which makes this the right moment to build a company, in my opinion.
The gap I saw is in how that transition is approached. PV is a demanding market: large R&D budgets are needed just to bring costs down, which squeezes margins. Silicon is now so cheap and reliable that competing with it head-on rarely makes sense. Many teams still aim at exactly that battle, often with funding structures that push them to scale before the product and market are ready.
There was also a personal reason. I had lived abroad for 11 years, and I saw a chance for a positive shift in Hungary. I wanted to help build deep-tech capability, skilled jobs and international visibility here, in my home country.
Nexunite works at the intersection of science, technology, business and funding. For a perovskite startup or research group, what does that look like in practice?
It means looking at a technology through several lenses at once: scientist, engineer, funder, investor, patent attorney and customer.
For the startups and research groups we support, that usually means:
matching their roadmap to the right funding calls;
shaping the concept and work packages;
finding partners and building the consortium;
writing the proposal, especially the impact, exploitation and IP sections;
supporting the project after it’s awarded.
Alongside that, we do patent landscaping and freedom-to-operate screening, and techno-economic assessments that show which materials and process steps really drive cost.
For Nexunite itself, it’s also our business model. Service revenue and public R&D funding cover part of the development risk. That makes our technology roadmap more resilient and means every euro invested goes further.
Many perovskite projects have promising lab results but face a long and expensive road to stable, scalable manufacturing. Where do you most often see them go wrong?
The most common mistake is picking the wrong battle. Going straight for outdoor power generation means racing silicon to the bottom on cost per kWh. A new technology can’t win that race without enormous capital, and thin-film PV has seen many well-funded companies struggle to turn investment into sales.
Reliability is the other big challenge, and it’s often underestimated. Perovskites are a new class of materials with their own degradation pathways. The testing standards developed for silicon don’t translate directly: passing the same tests doesn’t guarantee the same reliability in the field. Aging studies also take a long time, and you only learn what failed at the end of the test. Only then can you feed those findings back into your experiment design, so every learning cycle is slow and expensive.
That’s why we deliberately chose products that need shorter lifetimes than conventional outdoor modules. Indoor IoT devices run under much gentler conditions and have shorter service lives. That lets us bring real products to market sooner and keep learning from field data, while longer-lifetime applications mature in parallel.
What gaps did you see in how perovskite and other deep-tech innovations move from research to commercial deployment, and how does Nexunite address them?
Academia rewards papers and record numbers. Industry needs reproducibility, cost, reliability and a paying customer. In between sits a complex funding landscape and a European investor community that is understandably cautious with hardware deep tech. Many strong technologies stall in that space.
A second gap is fragmentation. Emerging PV players often develop the same things in parallel: the same materials, the same processes, the same solutions to the same stability problems. That spends private and taxpayer money several times over. Collaborative public funding such as Horizon Europe is where this can change. We’re happy to work with anyone, competitors included. If sustainable technology reaches the mass market, people and the planet win, and there’s more than enough room in the market for several successful companies.
Nexunite addresses both gaps in four ways:
A balanced business model
. Service revenue and public funding alongside equity, so investment speeds up a business that already stands on its own feet.
Niche markets with real value
. We target markets where we’re not judged on the cost of electricity. In indoor IoT, the value lies in replacing batteries and maintenance visits, enabled by light weight, flexibility and good low-light performance. Space and high-altitude applications come later, where power per gram matters most.
Manufacturability from day one
, using proven materials and equipment from our network.
Openness to collaboration
across the European ecosystem.
Over the years I’ve worked with people and companies along the whole value chain: material suppliers, equipment makers, research institutes, integrators and end users. That network is one of Nexunite’s biggest assets. We know which materials and tools work, and who to call, so we don’t start from scratch and can reach the market faster and at lower cost.
Where do you see Nexunite in three to five years?
On the technology side:
our own lab running in Budapest;
our first Horizon Europe projects, expected to start in January 2027, delivered successfully;
a pilot product at TRL 7, with flexible indoor modules built into real IoT applications.
On the services side, I’d like Nexunite to be a go-to partner in Europe for deep-tech teams building EU consortia and an IP strategy.
Above all, I want Nexunite to be a place where talented people want to work. Scientists and engineers should be able to work on exciting, meaningful problems while feeling secure, motivated and properly rewarded, including a share in the company’s success as it grows. We’re looking for talented scientists and engineers in perovskite device development, process engineering and coatings, so I’d be glad to hear from anyone who wants to help build this.
We’re also open to talking with investors who share this long-term view. Our foundation of services and public funding means investment can go straight into scale-up and product development rather than just keeping the lights on.

title: Self-forming microstructures boost lead-free near-infrared perovskite LEDs
content:
Self-forming microstructures boost lead-free near-infrared perovskite LEDs
Researchers at Nanjing University and Linköping University have developed lead-free CsSnI₃ perovskite LEDs that combine high radiance with improved operational stability in the near-infrared (NIR). The authors say the devices set a record for NIR tin-based perovskite LEDs and mark a substantial advance for solution-processed NIR optoelectronics.
Invisible NIR light sources are used in night-vision imaging, facial recognition and non-invasive biomedical sensing, but planar emitters with high optical output power remain difficult to make. The devices reach radiances of 6,304 W sr⁻¹ m⁻² under DC driving and 21,633 W sr⁻¹ m⁻² under pulsed driving, with a half-lifetime (T50) of 64.3 hours at a current density of 100 mA cm⁻².
The gains come from the spontaneous formation of discrete hemispherical perovskite microstructures in the emissive layer, which the team says improve both optical and thermal management. The researchers also used large-area planar LEDs to demonstrate night-vision surveillance without a visible red glow, along with biomedical imaging and sensing.
The work follows an
evaporated perovskite LED
that reached 25.0% external quantum efficiency in the near-infrared, from a Nanjing University-led team.

content:
The European Commission has approved a €9.5 billion Dutch state aid scheme
for the 2 GW IJmuiden Ver Gamma-A and IJmuiden Ver Gamma-B offshore wind
projects in the North Sea.
According to the Commission, the funding will support the Netherlands'
offshore wind deployment plans while advancing the European Union's objectives
under the Clean Industrial Deal.
Teresa Ribera, executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive
transition, said: "Today's decision unlocks €9.5 billion in Dutch
support for two major offshore wind projects in the North Sea, bringing
more clean electricity to the grid, cutting emissions and reducing our
reliance on imported fossil fuels."
Under the scheme, the Netherlands will organise two offshore wind tenders
years from the start of operations, which are currently scheduled for 2032.
Developers will be able to bid either to build the projects without state
aid and instead make a concession payment to the government for the site,
or to request an aid premium to support project development.
However, the Dutch government will only consider bids seeking an aid premium
if no developers submit offers that include a concession payment.
The European Commission approved the scheme after concluding that it is
necessary to support offshore wind development, that the aid provides an
incentive effect, and that it is proportionate due to the competitive bidding
process and safeguards built into the mechanism.
TGS | 4C Analyst Benedict Cooper commented: "EU approval of the Netherlands'
EUR 9.45bn TOWOZ state aid scheme is a key final step before the launch
of tender for the IJmuiden Ver Gamma A and B sites on 26 November."
"Bid submission will then be open until 10 December, with the award
expected to happen in Q1 2027, and will be the only tender run under the
temporary TOWOZ scheme prior to a shift to CfDs in 2027."
"This is an important moment for offshore wind in the Netherlands
and will be a key indication as to where the market is now, with the country
revamping its tender framework and reintroducing subsidies following the
failure of the Nederwiek I-A tender in 2025."

title: Aberdeen Chamber calls for action to protect Scotland's offshore wind pipeline
content:
The Aberdeen & Grampian Chamber of Commerce has released an eight point
plan that it says will restore confidence in the energy sector and protect
Scottish offshore wind projects.
The plan forms part of the chamber's 44th Energy Transition Survey, produced
in collaboration with Johnston Carmichael and D2Zero.
According to the report, increasingly unfavourable market conditions are
driving investment and resources out of the U.K.
David Wilson, Aberdeen office managing partner at Johnston Carmichael,
said: "The survey should be read as a warning to policymakers. Businesses
are making choices today about investment, recruitment and where to pursue
future growth."
The chamber is calling for measures to protect Scotland's offshore wind
pipeline through the U.K.'s Strategic Spatial Energy Plan, end the Energy
Profits Levy before 2030, increase investment in large-scale offshore projects
through Great British Energy and improve the efficiency of energy investment
decisions.
James Gaskell, chief executive officer of Hydrasun, a D2Zero company, said:
"Engineering expertise takes decades to develop. Once lost, it cannot
simply be recreated when the next major project arrives.
"Protecting that knowledge, attracting new talent and giving the next
generation confidence in a long-term career in energy must be priorities
for industry and government alike."

beta offshore converter platform in Germany.

grid connection project being developed in the German sector of the North
The project is part of TenneT’s ongoing expansion of offshore grid infrastructure

title: A Startup Emerges From Stealth With Highly Personalized AI
content: OpenAI’s ChatGPT remembers details of its users and what they look up, while Anthropic’s Claude Code uses its “auto memory” to take notes on users’ preferences and feedback. A new startup thinks AI models can get even more personalized. First Person Labs , founded seven months ago by two PhD students in the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory , a research institute at the university, is developing tech to make “user models,” the term for more personalized AI models and agents trained on an individual’s data. The startup is coming out of stealth Tuesday and has raised around $10 million in a funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz’s infrastructure team. “Any interface you talk to knows you,” Ken Liu , the company’s co-founder and CEO, said, adding that the company’s tech is “like a biographer—someone that follows you around and sees everything.” To do this, First Person Labs is making an agentic harness, or software infrastructure that wraps around a large language model. The harness—which the company has named Second , like second to one’s own consciousness—takes raw activity from your computer and makes inferences about you based upon it. For example, if your computer logs that you’re often writing at 2 a.m., the model will infer that you’re a night owl. It then constructs a personalized model of what you do and how you think. (Harnesses have also been used by a handful of large tech companies, like Uber , to help them swap between AI models to cut costs .) The company uses a mixture of open-source models like GLM , DeepSeek and Jev as well as some close-source models like Gemini and OpenAI for its harness. It uses this mixture because some inputs don’t require sophisticated models, whereas understanding the intent behind a particular action, like why you worded a delicate email in a particular way, might necessitate some analysis from Anthropic’s high-intelligence model Fable , for instance. Liu said the company plans to generate revenue through subscriptions rather than advertising. The company will be “no ads, forever,” Liu said, because he thinks ads would detract from the personalized feel of the product. Like a personal assistant, people will mostly interact with Second by chatting with it. They can also connect Second directly to other apps, like OpenAI’s Dot , Meta’s Muse and Instinct . Liu thinks First Person Labs’ Second will be able to use the data it collects about you to help these tools arrive at better, more personal results, faster: For example, if your personal assistant knew when school vacation started, it could more seamlessly help you book flights. “Existing personal assistants…can do things, but they don't know you,” he said. “So for user models, it’s almost exclusively focused on the context—understanding you so deeply, and then serving that understanding elsewhere.” First Person Labs lets its individual users control their data, including determining what their Second can and can’t be trained on, and choose which models they’d like their Second to use. That was important to Liu, who researched the intersection of AI and data privacy in his computer science PhD at Stanford, as well as the startup’s investors at Andreessen Horowitz. “As we weave AI into our lives it will come to learn the most sensitive things about us,” Andreessen Horowitz partner Joel de la Garza said. “We invested in First Person Labs because they treat that as an architectural question rather than a policy question, they give control to the user, and we deeply believe that is the right answer.” Here’s what else is going on… People on the Move: Jason Wei Jason Wei , a high-profile AI researcher who worked on OpenAI’s reasoning and deep research models before joining Meta Superintelligence Labs in July 2025, is now joining data curation firm Mercor as its first chief scientist, Wei told The Information exclusively. Wei will be focused on building out an AI research team at the startup. Specifically, he hopes to build more benchmarks that focus on economically valuable tasks in areas like accounting, legal, health and finance, as well as benchmarks for areas in which AI models are rapidly improving and potentially exceeding human capabilities, such as software engineering and the ability for AI to conduct AI research. Wei also said that Mercor wants to conduct research into how to improve model post-training, or the process of tweaking models after they’re already trained. The startup hopes to help business customers cheaply specialize open-source models using their own data for their own specific applications, Wei said. title: Why the Road to an IPO Is Getting Longer
content: Trillion-dollar-plus IPOs may be stealing the headlines, but for companies hoping to launch that aren’t Anthropic or SpaceX, the path to public markets looks less certain. Companies that have spent years getting IPO-ready may have to wait longer to launch as market conditions shift yet again. To explore how companies can prepare for an IPO in an unpredictable climate, The Information reporter Dakin Campbell spoke to three investment experts about the long road to going public. Kiran Choudary, chief financial officer, Rubrik Crystal Shen, head of West Coast capital markets, NYSE Kate Claassen, managing director, chairman of global internet banking, Morgan Stanley The Road to Readiness Successful IPOs, said Kate Claassen, should be market-ambivalent. “It’s more about being a successful public company on days when markets go up and when markets go down,” she said, adding that success means having alignment with investors on strategy and the metrics that point to it working. Kiran Choudary knows first hand how long the road can be. Rubrik began preparing for an IPO in late 2022 but didn’t go public until early 2024, after a prolonged slowdown in the IPO market. Choudary broke preparation into three stages. The first is business readiness: having the scale, executive team and durable growth story to appeal to investors. The second is financial and risk infrastructure, including clean audits and an audit committee. The third is the IPO process itself: working with the Securities and Exchange Commission, bankers and lawyers, and testing the waters with investors. “Since 2022, there’s never really been a solidly open window,” Choudary said. Instead, there have been short periods when a handful of companies go public before activity slows again. “If you want to be a public company, if your business is ready and you feel good about it, you have to find a reasonable window and go.” The Early-Bird Advantage More companies are staying private for longer, in part because they have the option of raising capital and growing outside the public markets. The NYSE is responding by getting involved earlier in companies’ IPO journeys, sometimes as early as Series A, giving them access to the exchange’s resources and its network of 2,400 publicly listed companies. “A lot of times, we’re hosting events where private issuers can get exposure to their publicly listed counterparts. That’s exposure to potential end-market customers,” said Crystal Shen. “You leave a lot on the table if you wait until the very end to engage with an exchange.” Investors need the same early attention, said Claassen, who advised companies to build relationships with major IPO investors years before a roadshow begins. Existing investors who know a company well are more likely to participate in its IPO and remain significant shareholders afterward. “Data does show that the longer an investor’s been with you, the longer they’re going to stick with you,” she said. Even decisions made during a company’s earliest funding rounds can have consequences much later. Shen pointed to index inclusion, which can hinge on how a company is positioned in registration statements and how much of its stock is available for public trading. Voting rights in the hands of unrestricted investors, for example, can affect eligibility for indexes such as the Russell US Equity. “That should shape how you structure some of your private rounds to ensure you have [the] appropriate float for index inclusion down the line,” Shen said. The Changing IPO Landscape As companies spend longer in private markets, raising more capital and growing larger before going public, IPOs are getting bigger. The funds investing in them are growing, too. “The large funds are getting larger, and it’s creating this cycle,” Shen said, noting that smaller and mid-cap funds are declining in both number and assets. That makes it harder for smaller companies to attract institutional investors. Choudary agreed, recalling that when he was a banker, software companies with $100 million to $150 million in revenue could go public. “In tech, I don’t think that sized company going public even exists anymore,” he said. The pressure doesn’t end at the IPO. Claassen said the biggest challenge is volatility between listing and the end of the lockup period, which can hit employees’ tax bills. Shen added that how companies structure tender offers, in which shares are bought from existing holders, can have repercussions later on. Those programs often let only current employees and certain early investors sell, leaving other investors and former employees to find liquidity once the company goes public. That, she said, creates pent-up supply ahead of the IPO. “Companies and management teams need to think about that increased level of secondary activity pre-IPO,” Shen said, “to alleviate some of those issues you’re going to have post-IPO.”

title: AMD and Google Chip Away at Nvidia as Huang Exit Shakes Customers
content: Even before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week, AI chips from smaller rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices were starting to win converts. Huang’s departure is likely to reinforce that shift in sentiment. Cirrascale, a 16-year-old cloud provider that operates 25 data centers, started fielding significant interest last year from customers interested in running AI workloads on AMD’s specialized AI chip, according to CEO David Driggers. He said AMD’s chips are particularly suited for running AI models—the process known as inference—which is becoming more popular among businesses. “I’d say the first two years of the company, it was like chewing glass to convince the customer that AMD was a viable option,” said Piotr Tomasik, chief operating officer of Tensorwave, a young cloud provider backed by AMD that runs the company’s chips. Last year, things turned around as outside research showed AMD’s chips being comparable or better than Nvidia on some benchmarks. Google, AMD, Amazon and a host of up-and-coming chip startups have been trying to unseat Nvidia’s dominance in the market for graphics processing units for years. Those efforts are finally starting to bear fruit, in part due to improvements in the rivals’ chips’ performance and their lower cost at a time when Nvidia chips are still expensive and hard to come by. Since late 2025, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have said that they would use AMD’s chips to run their AI models (earlier this week, OpenAI said it would use TensorWave’s cloud). Nvidia’s ability to play defense has likely been weakened by last week’s departure of Jensen Huang as CEO, after reports of multiple affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, came to light. The board tapped Nvidia chief financial officer Collette Kress as an interim replacement for Huang. To be sure, Nvidia remains far ahead of AMD and others in terms of its business. Nvidia projected revenue of $108 billion for its fiscal third quarter, which it is reporting Tuesday night, about eight times AMD’s third-quarter revenue reported on Nov. 3. History shows that a successor CEO to a high-profile personality can sometimes outperform the better-known person. Tim Cook, for instance, built Apple into a much bigger company than it had been under Steve Jobs. But Daniel Svonava, CEO at inference provider Superlinked, which specializes in running open-source models, said that in the wake of Kress’s appointment he is less confident that Nvidia will invest enough to make more of its chips available. “CFOs are not known to be very aggressive in the capital deployment, which is what needs to happen to meet the demand to alleviate the compute crunch,” Svonava said. “This latest Nvidia news is the final nail in the coffin for us to switch from experimenting to real deployment.” Cost-Effective Svonava’s company had been testing AMD chips for a few months but began to take them more seriously in recent months, after small open-weight AI models were released from firms like DeepSeek. AMD’s chips are ideal to run such models, he said. AMD chips are much cheaper than Nvidia’s, which makes running some models with AMD chips a higher-margin business for Superlinked. AMD has also managed to improve its RocM software, according to Tomasik, which developers use to program AI models to work on AMD chips. RocM is AMD’s response to Nvidia’s Cuda software, whose popularity with programmers has long been an Nvidia advantage. Before these improvements, TensorWave had dedicated staff to help customers figure out AMD’s software. Tomasik said the amount of time staffers have to spend helping customers crackROCm has dropped 80% to 90% since last year. ROCm’s improvements could give AMD more opportunity to dislodge CUDA. Interest in AMD is helping cloud firms running on AMD chips. TensorWave expects to be generating revenue at an annualized recurring rate of $210 million by the end of 2026, compared to $125 million at the end of 2025. Another AMD-focused cloud provider Sciforium has tripled its customer base since June, when it signed its first commercial contract, and in the past year has grown its capacity five-fold and nearly tripled its team, said CEO Hassan Akbari. The startup, which AMD has invested in, is raising additional funding to add more capacity, Akbari said. Google Google has been spending heavily to expand the market for its TPU AI chips, including by helping finance the building of data centers that will use the chips outside Google Cloud. In July, the company revealed it had agreed to cover as much as $44 billion in data center lease backstops, under which Google would be on the hook if the tenant defaults. Cirrascale recently became one of the first providers of Google’s TPUs outside of Google Cloud. Already, customers have signaled interest in spending hundreds of millions of dollars on computing using Google’s TPU 8 chip, Driggers said. More companies that rely on Nvidia’s chips are starting to use Google’s TPUs. Last month, for instance, The Information reported that Google would sell its TPU chips to OpenAI—the same day Oracle announced it would offer the chips to its own customers. Google has also said it has updated its software to make it easier for customers to run TPUs. The autonomous delivery platform Autolane has primarily used GPUs on Google Cloud but since September, has started moving workflows, like evaluations, to TPUs, Chad Agate, the company’s cofounder and chief technology officer told The Information. The company is now considering heavier, more complex workloads for TPUs, citing a lower cost, Agate said. “We’re looking at moving more workloads, it’s promising,” he said, noting that the company is still heavily reliant on GPUs. “We’re not abandoning ship, we’re looking at which workloads make sense.” TPUs still pale in comparison to Nvidia’s chips. Of the cloud software firm DoiT’s roughly 5,000 customers, only 16 are using TPUs in “real volume,” Vadim Solovey, the CEO of the company said. “These chips are a second supplier, not a replacement.” Nvidia’s Edge Nvidia still has a litany of advantages that rivals must contend with. Because of its large production volumes, Nvidia gets priority for manufacturing capacity during supply crunches from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the dominant manufacturer of AI chips, The Information has previously reported . As a result of that relationship, Nvidia chips remain plentifully available, some customers have found. One startup founder said they were in talks to rent the newest AMD chips at the beginning of this year, but learned they could only get access to the chips by the end of this year at the earliest. Because the startup could get comparable Nvidia chips sooner, it ultimately walked away from using AMD, the founder said. The first time a customer of cloud provider Megaport asked to use AMD chips to run AI workloads was three or four months ago, driven by the difficulty of securing Nvidia chips, said CEO Michael Reid. But the customer would have had to wait six months to get the AMD chips, whereas the lead time for Nvidia chips was 12 to 14 weeks, Reid said, so the customer decided not to use AMD. Nvidia has also built up a robust sales and marketing organization that goes above and beyond traditional vendor relations, an advantage that industry executives say rivals like AMD still cannot match. “Nvidia has been the most proactive vendor I’ve ever worked with in my life,” Reid said. “Nvidia is the only one I’ve ever worked with who will help you with customers, who will help you like they try to connect you with finance people, they try to find you data centers. The rest of them do nothing.” Driggers said that his customers were still increasing their orders of Nvidia chips. Even so, he said, “Nvidia is still dominating, but … they’re losing market percentage.”

title: OpenAI’s Astra Is a Boon to Robotics, Says Nvidia Robotics Chief Deepu Talla
content: When OpenAI released its Astra model in September, users quickly found that it excelled at tasks that require understanding the physical world. One of those most impressed by its performance was Nvidia’s robotics chief Deepu Talla, who told The Information it is a breakthrough in efforts to create robots that can handle a wide variety of jobs. Astra has made it 100 times faster to create some kinds of data for training robotic AI models and could help automate the process of putting robots to work in factories, Talla said on the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. (The full episode, which was recorded before Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO, is available here .) “The Astra moment happened, where agents are now truly able to basically use all the physical AI tools that are available—whether it’s for simulation, whether it’s for training,” he said. As a result, the ability to create useful robots is on “completely a different rocket ship than where we were a year ago.” Among Astra’s physical-world feats, it could model mechanical parts using engineering software, and it outperformed some specialized robotics AI models when controlling robot arms. One person even gave an Astra-powered robot a canvas and brushes, and the model painted scenes of the Golden Gate bridge. Roboticists have long relied on computer simulations to train AI models to power robots, but that approach was in part limited by the speed of creating simulated versions of the objects the robot might interact with and the environment it would work in, which could take months. Thanks to Astra’s ability to automate that process, new robotic AI models trained in simulations and released over the next 6-to-12 months will be able to work with much higher accuracy than today’s leading models, Talla predicted. Running those simulations requires AI chips like the ones Nvidia designs, which are also used in training AI models and running them on robots. Talla also discussed the three speeds at which robots have to think, why he expects a ‘ChatGPT moment for robotics’ in the next 1-to-3 years and the role for humanoid robots in manufacturing. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Deepu Talla. Deepu is Vice President of Robotics and Edge AI at Nvidia. Deepu, welcome on the show. Talla: Rocket, how are you? Drew: I’m doing well. How are you? Talla: Great, thank you. Drew: I’m really excited for this conversation. I think there’s a lot happening in robotics and physical AI is such a hot topic right now. It’s always a pleasure to talk to you about this. So excited to get into it. Talla: Yeah, looking forward to it. Drew: Well, one thing that just happened is Nvidia had its developer conference in Berlin, GTC Berlin. You were there, is that right? Talla: That’s right. Drew: How was Berlin? Talla: I mean, Berlin was amazing. I mean, if you think about some of the toughest problems we have to solve as a human race. We’ve been trying to solve robotics, physical AI, for a long time. As you know, automation has been around for 50 plus years, right? And the technology was not good enough until recently we reached a tipping point. And what was so exciting in Germany? Obviously, a lot of German companies were there, but also a lot of European companies from the region. A lot of the deployments there are tailored towards small and medium manufacturing enterprises. If you think about Europe, Germany, Mittelstand, it’s really small and medium precision, super specialized applications. And robotics, the technology was never really good enough to be deployed in an autonomous manner, and because these are small and medium enterprises, the jobs tend to be extremely high mix. So you can never really program a robot to work in those kind of environments. So you need really autonomous capability, and now the technology is reasonably maturing to address those type of problems. Literally, I mean it felt like all of Europe, everybody working on all the startups, all the researchers, all the developers, large companies, everybody was in Berlin. It was supremely vibrant for me. Drew: You mean to actually do the deployment autonomously, to do the integration work? That that’s something that has to happen autonomously, or to get automation in place. Talla: Yeah. So there’s two parts to it, right? First of all, the intelligence in order to do a task or a set of tasks needs to be good enough. Good enough meaning it needs to be accurate. It needs to be reliable. Do it all the time the same way. And it needs to be safe (and economical and so on). So that general purpose brain that can comprehend the physical world, the environment, we haven’t reached that tipping point yet. Like what happened in November 2022 with ChatGPT for the digital world. So the best in the world from researchers to developers to labs, everybody is trying to work towards that problem of making that physical AI brain accurate enough. That’s the first step. Now, once you are able to create that brain, you still need to deploy that brain into specific robot embodiments into existing workflows, and that’s a fairly complicated endeavor as well because program you can’t program the robot, and they need to work with other robots of different capabilities, they need to work with digital AIs, and of course, they also need to work with humans. So that integration step is not easy because it’s going to be custom on a case by case basis. So that technology was not available either until suddenly, like a month or so ago, the Astra moment happened, where agents are now truly able to basically use all the physical AI tools that are available, whether it’s for simulation, whether it’s for training, whether it’s for runtime deployment, and they’re able to iteratively take good robot brains and see if they can integrate into existing workflows. So progress on both fronts is necessary. Number one, the general purpose brain is accurate, reliable and safe. Number two, you can integrate that into existing workflows. Drew: The importance and the significance of that integration work, I imagine, is something that’s really salient for people in these traditional manufacturing centers in Europe. On the West Coast, here in California, there’s a kind of AI arrogance, sometimes that AI is everything. That’s the only important part of the problem. I mean, is there something that roboticists here in California stand to learn from traditional manufacturers in Europe? Talla: Yeah, I don’t know if it’s we are being in the Silicon Valley we are being, how would I say, too brave or too proud—I don’t think it’s that. What really it is is again, there’s two parts to the puzzle, right? Since we haven’t really solved the general purpose accuracy in the first place, we really never had to go and solve the integration problem at scale. So the integration problem is really scaling out the intelligence. But luckily, the whole agentic AI revolution—Gee, what was it? Just happened in February of this year in the digital world. And that advance is going incredibly fast now. And just when Astra was released, we were pleasantly surprised. I for sure was because what we were doing, in order to train the robot brain, for example, you have this lot of data collection that’s required. As you know, in the physical world, the accuracy requirement is much higher than the digital world. And what was happening was we had to basically collect lots of real world data, and that’s kind of happening. But that was not going to be sufficient. So synthetic data generation was an obvious concept, but the problem with synthetic data generation was that you needed artists or needed CAD models to create accurate 3D representations of all the different objects and the spaces. And as much as AI has progressed, still creating those environments and those assets was extremely time-consuming to the point of several months. If you wanted to create a digital twin of an environment, it would take several months, including using generative AI to do that. Now, suddenly, what happened with this agentic AI, like Astra, for example, was trained on the physical world. It has a good idea of the physics of the world, it has a good idea of the space and time relationship, what you call spatial-temporal relationship. So, because of that, it is able to basically study the properties of the objects. It’s going to go on the internet and probably pull out a CAD that may be available from it, or from a picture or a video, which need not be a full, accurate 3D scan per se, but just by taking some pictures and video, it’s able to construct those environments. Which essentially means what used to take months in generating synthetic assets and environments suddenly got 100X boost and speed up. Which means now suddenly we can use that capability, agentic AI capability, to create good data to train our models better, faster, to converge faster, to increase the intelligence. So that’s the number one observation. And then number two, equally important, if you had a reasonably good enough brain that you can deploy for whatever application, that integration work—typically, imagine you have to put it in a factory. The factory, there’s machines. Some of them are controlled by PLCs that might be 20–30 year old. Most likely it is, and they have some bespoke, programming language to control that. And sometimes you have to connect that to a ERP system. If you’re talking about the supply chain. It might have to be connected to a building management system, so on so forth, right? So who’s writing all that glue code? It’s actually pretty boring to write the glue code. There’s not that many people actually who know that, and the manuals are all out there somewhere. But if you throw agents at them, and the agents are actually able to study all those manuals and understand all the glue code and write it, that’s another 100X lift, I think. So because while you’re trying to create intelligence, the pre-work has gotten 100X better. The post-work, which is basically the deployment, has gotten 100X better. Now suddenly, the pace at which we can create useful physical AI intelligence is, I think, we are on a completely a different rocket ship than where we were a year ago. Drew: Yeah, I think both of those are really great examples of ways that LLMs are removing bottlenecks to deployment, and in kind of unintuitive ways. Like I don’t know if people would have appreciated how useful it is to be able to develop these sim-ready assets using a model like OpenAI’s Astra. Why do you think Astra got so good at that capability? Why now is it all of a sudden really good at CAD and Blender and this physical understanding? Talla: I think the first modality that was being solved in the last three to five years was all about language, and then when language got added, and a couple of years ago video got added and other sensors got added. But however, I think this is just the next evolution, right? Physical AI quite simply is the largest opportunity. As language has gotten good, as video’s gotten good, now it’s about combining all of those to solve spatiotemporal problems. And I think I actually believe that they actually did a good job of training the model to actually do this very type of tasks that we really need to be solved. Drew: I see. It was a deliberate decision. OpenAI decided the time is right to target these physical capabilities, and so maybe they went out and bought a lot of reinforcement learning environments to train those CAD capabilities. But they targeted this capability. Talla: Yeah, I didn’t ask them explicitly, but my guess is it didn’t happen accidentally, but it was really interesting to solve this sort of a problem. Drew: Yeah, that would be my guess too. So my question—I think both of these are real accelerants: using LLMs to create these simulation assets, using LLMs to write that kind of glue code to enable faster deployment. The question that comes to mind for me, though, is is that really the hardest part of the problem? Even if we were able to use LLMs to automate that and make that as fast as possible, aren’t there other bottlenecks or other frictions that are going to still get in the way? For example, dealing with the IT guy at the factory, getting the IT person to agree to put the robots on the Wi-Fi. That’s a very human problem that LLMs, I don’t know if they’re going to solve that. Talla: Yeah, you’re right. The thing to remember is, we have several orders of magnitude improvement needed before you go and deploy these things at scale. For example, what’s a good accuracy in the digital world, if your model is 90, 95% accurate, that’s a pretty good accuracy because in most cases in the digital world, especially if it relates to consumer type of applications, it’s more of a hint and there’s a human in the loop to close the last 5 or 10%. In the physical world, it’s not about 90, 95; it’s 99-point how many nines of accuracy do you need after that? Because in almost all cases, there’s no human in the loop. So, if you think from that perspective, in where we are today and where we need to go, 100X improvement is very good. But let’s say you’re at 99, it basically means that you went from 99 to 99.99. That’s impressive. But you need to get to 99 point maybe six nines or eight nines. So we need lot of these step function exponentials that are happening. So I think what happened right now with respect to LLMs agents solving the asset creation and also the post is a step in the right direction, necessary but not sufficient. To your point, right?
